Input: If we accept that dark matter exist, they must be part of the entire planet Earth, including living plant and animal organisms. In this case, is it correct to believe that dark matter is part of the human organism? If dark matter exists, it is indeed presumed to be present everywhere, though its density is very low compared to terrestrial densities. However, I’d hesitate to call it a “part of”, e.g., organisms. By way of an example that is known to exist with certainty, right now there are countless neutrinos going through your body. Are they part of your body? Not really. Why? Because neutrinos are effectively non-interacting. To them, your body might as well not be there. And vice versa, for your body the presence of the neutrinos makes no difference. Neutrinos still interact with ordinary matter though, just very, very, very weakly. An awful lot of neutrinos would be needed to make a noticeable difference. Sure, if you happened to be situated near an exploding supernova, the neutrino flux might be enough to evaporate you in an instant, but for that, the explosion of an entire giant star would be required, fairly close to you. In contrast, the millions, billions, trillions of neutrinos that pass through your body right this moment make no difference whatsoever. They are not part of you. The presumed dark matter of cosmology interacts even less with ordinary matter. So even if it is present right here, right now, it is not part of you, of animals, plants, or the Earth. It happens to be in the same place in space at the same time, but it might as well be in another galaxy far, far away: There is no interaction, no connection between that dark matter medium and your body. So no, whether or not dark matter exists remains to be seen, but it is definitely not part of the human body. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If the “one-way” speed of light hasn’t yet been measured and we can just affirm the average 2-way speed of light for all points & perspectives is what measures c, what does that mean for ancient nighttime stars we see, that light’s not from long ago? Questions like this pop up regularly, and they are not silly. However, it is important to understand that ultimately, we do not measure speed, one-way, two-way or otherwise. We also do not measure distances. The only “pure” measurement that we can do without hidden assumptions is counting the ticks of a reliable clock. Of course even this measurement is based on an important assumption: Namely that in this universe, reliable clocks exist. Clocks that tick in sync; clocks that, when brought apart and later brought back together, will still continue to tick in sync (though they may have counted a different number of ticks in the meantime, while they were apart). All other measurements are derived from clock ticks. But… rulers! Oh, if idealized rulers existed… Well, then we wouldn’t have relativity theory, would we! An idealized ruler is perfectly rigid. Move one end and the other end moves instantaneously, no matter how far it is from the first! Spin the ruler at one end, and the other end will move around rapidly, perhaps many times faster than the vacuum speed of light! No such thing exists. Real rulers are physical objects, and when you move them around, different parts move at different speeds, depending on the material properties of the ruler, the speed of sound in that material and such things. In the end, the only way to properly calibrate a ruler is, you guessed it, by using a clever arrangement of reliable clocks and light signals. Yes, light signals. Because when two clocks are apart, we have no other means of relating their readings. So for instance, when we calibrate a ruler, we can attach a clock to one end, send a light signal to the other end and let it return, and then use the time elapsed on that clock to infer the length of the ruler. We can repeat this experiment using a clock on the other end, even a clock in the middle, but ultimately this is all we have: clocks and light signals. So we really have to turn things upside down. Forget about measuring the speed of light; assume that the vacuum speed of light is universal, then make a bunch of measurements, and check if the results are consistent with that assumption. They are. Of course you are free to propose alternatives. You are free to propose an alternative theory in which the speed of light is not constant, depends on direction, etc., and see if you can come up with results that are consistent with observation. However, unless your proposal is conceptually simpler than special relativity, do not be surprised if it is not received with enthusiasm. When two theories yield identical predictions, we generally prefer the one that’s simpler. And special relativity has a whole bunch of other factors supporting it, not the least the fact that Maxwell’s beautiful equations found a “native home” in four-dimensional spacetime, on account of the fact that the vacuum equations are conformally invariant in such a spacetime, and even in the presence of charges, the theory remains invariant under the Lorentz-Poincaré group. So for electromagnetism alone, special relativity is the native “playground”. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What is a photon? Is it an object? I ask because photons are always moving at lightspeed, and no object can reach lightspeed. Well, technically, an “object” can travel at the vacuum speed of light (in fact, only at the vacuum speed of light) if it has no rest mass. In that case, the dispersion relation E 2 = ( m c 2 ) 2 + ( p c ) 2 becomes just E = p c , that is, the momentum and energy of the object are proportional to one another. Of course an “object”, or test particle, is just an abstraction of classical physics. We know that such things do not exist in a quantum reality. Nor are electrons, photons, etc., “objects”. Even in ordinary quantum mechanics, they are not miniature cannonballs: they are characterized not by positions or momenta but by states, which may translate into specific position or momentum values under the right circumstances that we perhaps call a measurement, but most of the time, the states are more complicated than that. But ordinary quantum mechanics really doesn’t know about photons. For that, we need quantum field theory, in the form of quantum electrodynamics. We know from Maxwell’s theory that far away from charges, in otherwise empty space, influences in the electromagnetic field travel as plane waves at the invariant velocity c . (This invariance is what inspired special relativity after all). In the quantum field theory, the energy of these waves can only increase or decrease by predetermined units, or quanta. When something interacts with the electromagnetic field, this increase or decrease registers, or can be interpreted as, the emission or the absorption of a particle. We call these quanta or particles photons. So what travels at the vacuum speed of light is, well, light, electromagnetic waves far away from sources (charges). Particle-like behavior is observed when these waves are emitted or absorbed, leading us to the mental model of thinking of a ray of light as a bunch of photons (which is misleading since we know for a fact since the beginning of the 19th century, the famous Arago-spot and all, that light is a wave, not corpuscular in nature). Short story: Particles in quantum field theory are not miniature cannonballs, but unit excitations of fields. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Are atheists aware that they're about to go to hell for quadrillions of years? In hell, you get tormented everyday. Suppose you are right. Suppose there is an afterlife, and a day comes when we are judged, with our souls perhaps condemned to eternity. Am I going to be judged by my deeds? Sure, I made mistakes. To quote the immortal Sinatra, regrets I’ve had a few, but then again, too few to mention. And yes, there were times when I bit off more than I could chew. But I ate it up, faced it all, and, well, did my best to stand tall. Will your favorite deity or deities then judge me by my deeds? By how I lived my life? In that case, I have little to fear. Or is your deity a shallow, vain hypocrite? Someone who cares not how you lived your life, only takes church attendance? Who offers an afterlife where those who proclaim their “love of god” win because no matter what sins they commit, so long as they dutifully arrive for Sunday service, all is forgiven? Well, if that’s your deity, I say bugger him. I’d rather spend an eternity in hell than be a sycophant in a tyrant’s court. But you know what? I think you have it wrong. At least if you are of the Christian persuasion. Read some Dante. Consider what happens in his vision of hell. Compare the fate of the virtuous pagans — folks who are in hell for the sin of not acknowledging Christ, either through no fault of their own (newborn, folks who lived before Christ or in far-off lands) or folks who rejected Christ for reasons of conscience — against the fate of hypocrites, including numerous popes. The sole punishment of the virtuous pagans is that they don’t enjoy God’s presence. Otherwise, they are untouched by Satan. The hypocrites, in turn, ended up in one of the deepest pits of hell. Or going back further, think of the Old Testament, the roots of all Abrahamic religions, the story of how humans were cast out of the Garden of Eden. Humans who were created in “God’s image”, which is to say, endowed with free will. A free will that was then tested when Satan tempted them to eat the forbidden fruit: Fruit from the tree of knowledge, knowledge to tell good and evil apart. In other words: a conscience. This Abrahamic god is not interested in blind obedience or church attendance. He is wiser than that. He is interested in how you listen to your conscience. And that’s why I do not fear your imaginary afterlife. Because even though I do not believe in deities or a supernatural afterlife, I know enough about the Abrahamic family of religions to know that God does not rule by fear. If you allow yourself to be guided by fear of hell, you are already on the wrong path, of that I am certain. And that is true whether or not God actually exists.

Can you explain the calculation for determining the time it takes for an object to fall into a black hole while traveling at the speed of light? First of all, you have to disabuse yourself of the notion that an object is traveling at a speed of… whatever. Speed is not an inherent property. The theory of relativity is called relativity for a reason: Speed is always relative. It is a relationship between two reference frames. So let us look at an hapless traveler falling into a black hole. What is that traveler’s speed? Well, as I just said, it is meaningless to speak of that traveler’s speed as an inherent property. The traveler’s speed depends on who is looking. OK, so we are looking. From some safe position outside the black hole’s event horizon. What do we see? Why, we see the traveler approach the place where the horizon will presumably form. Except that, the closer he gets to that place, the slower he appears to us, due to extreme gravitational time dilation. In fact, we literally (and I mean literally, not some figure-of-speech) never get to see the traveler actually reach the horizon. That moment — indeed, the moment when the horizon forms in the first place — remains for us forever in the future, due to extreme, runaway gravitational time dilation. And this is where we have a paradoxical situation. We know that the traveler reaches the vacuum speed of light at the horizon; that’s how black holes work. But from our perspective, the traveler’s speed actually drops to zero because of extreme gravitational time dilation! Well, guess what: in our reference frame, the speed of anything, including light itself, drops to zero at the horizon. Except that “the horizon” is not a place here and now, but a moment in time in our infinite future: Which is to say, we will see things slow down, slow down exponentially, but the moment when the horizon forms, the moment when all those speeds reach zero in our reference frame, will forever remain in our future. In fact, in our reference frame there is no meaningful way to describe the horizon or what’s “inside”. That’s why the darn thing is actually called a “horizon”! OK, what about the traveler’s perspective, then? Well, apart from increasing tides, he’d experience nothing special if he’s not looking out through the portholes of his spaceship. If the black hole is very, very large, tidal forces won’t be excessive even as he approaches, and crosses, the horizon. But he is doomed: he is now in a mini-universe that is collapsing around him, with no means of escape unless he has a time machine, because for him, the horizon has now become a moment of time in the past, and the only way to escape, to cross the horizon backwards, is by traveling into the past. In due course his mini-universe collapses and the world ends. The calculations are not elementary but not particularly hard either. The key equation is the so-called geodesic equation that describes freefalling trajectories. To model things from the traveler’s perspective, we need a coordinate system that covers both the interior and the exterior of the event horizon; one such coordinate system is called Kruskal—Szekeres coordinates. Whatever coordinate system we pick, we can calculate the “proper time”, i.e., the amount of time the traveler would measure, to reach the event horizon of the black hole and to reach the singularity (i.e., the “end of the world” for the mini-universe enclosed by the horizon.) Lastly, I hasten to add that this is classical relativity. Once we introduce quantum physics, things change, since black holes evaporate in finite time, so the traveler may never experience the horizon in the first place. But that’s a different story. Dumb question of the day: If we compressed a single gram of matter to the point of creating a black hole, would it sink to the Earth's core and eventually absorb the entire planet? What would happen, how would it progress and how long would it take? Well, for starters, even if there was a known method to compress matter in such small quantities to densities far exceeding the density even in the interior of the densest neutron star, it would likely require energy far in excess of the 1 gram rest mass-energy of the matter that we started with. OK, so maybe we can start with 0.1 grams or whatever, so in the end, we create a 1 gram black hole after investing an insane amount of energy by a yet-to-be-discovered process. Well, that black hole would not last very long. It would release all its energy in 0.0000000000000000000000000465 seconds, give or take, mostly in the form of gamma radiation that would be at least ten orders of magnitude more energetic than the particle energies in the Large Hadron Collider. These gamma photons would of course be absorbed by whatever is nearby, resulting in extreme heat and ultimately a thermal explosion with a power comparable to that of the Hiroshima bomb. Kaboom! But suppose we got this all wrong and there is no Hawking radiation; so once created, our 1 gram black hole is eternal. It would indeed fall through the floor and… well, not so much sink as fall freely towards the center of the Earth, interacting only infrequently with the atoms it runs across during its journey. Why? Because it would be insanely, insanely small. Something like 15 orders of magnitude smaller than a proton. And its supposedly enormous gravity? Not that enormous if you think about it unless you get very, very, very close. You’d have to be within less than one tenth of a micron from this black hole to experience 1 g acceleration. Would this 1 gram black hole accrete matter? Yes, it would. I calculated its so-called Bondi accretion rate assuming it’s sinking in a nonrelativistic medium with a density ten times that of water and a speed of sound of 1000 m/s, which is probably not a gross misrepresentation of the Earth’s interior. Long story short, assuming I used my calculator correctly, it would take roughly 10 billion times the present age of the universe… for the 1 g black hole to double in size and become a 2 g black hole.

Classical physics says objects move because they were pushed. Quantum physics says objects tunnel spontaneously (and not pushed by anything). how can this difference be resolved? Actually, neither of the statements in the question are correct, but let me get down to details. Classical physics says that the motion of an object may change (i.e., it accelerates) if a force acts on that object. Motion requires no pushing. A change in motion requires pushing. This was historically not evident to humans until early modern times, since it seemed that, for all practical intents and purposes, motion ceased unless things were pushed continuously. It was not until Newton and others that we learned that this cessation of motion required a force as well: the force of friction, air resistance or other “dissipative” forces that turned the macroscopic motion of objects into the microscopic motion (rotation, vibration, etc.) of particles that we recognize as (waste) heat. What quantum physics says is not that “objects tunnel”. Nothing of the sort. Tunneling is about states, not objects. A system’s state may be characterized, among other things, by its energy-content. In classical physics, a system may lose energy to its environment if a lower energy state is available, but it does not happen if achieving that lower energy state first requires climbing to higher energy state, i.e., climbing over a (fictitious) “barrier”. This really should not be terribly mysterious. A piece of wood is in a higher energy state than the ashes and smoke that it turns into when it burns. Yet wood does not combust spontaneously. That is because its higher energy state is metastable. We need to invest energy (light it on fire with a match) in order to overcome the energy barrier before the wood can combust on its own and turn into ashes and smoke, with the excess energy released as heat. And this is what tunneling is about: a quantum system may overcome that barrier even in the absence of a push. We picture this as the system “borrowing” energy from the vacuum but I caution against reading this too literally. What it basically means is that something that is impossible in classical physics is simply improbable in the quantum world. However, and this must be stressed, the quantum world may be probabilistic in nature but conservation laws, including the law of energy conservation, are not. They hold exactly even in the world of quantum physics. That energy barrier? The system never exists as an observable system in a transitional state with more energy than it began with. The system can be observed before tunneling and after tunneling, with the released energy in some other form (again, for instance, waste heat).

Why were the breakthroughs in the development of physics from 1900 to 1935 far greater than subsequent period? It seems that those 35 years were the period of the greatest explosion in the development of physics in the entire science history. Is the premise of this question really valid? Permit me to challenge it. Certainly, the first one third of the 20th century saw not one but two extraordinary revolutions in physics, the development of relativity theory and that of the quantum theory. But similar, profound revolutions have taken place previously. Perhaps the biggest, I’d argue, something even more profound than the development of quantum physics and relativity, was the shift from the Aristotelian to the modern view of the physical world. In Aristotle’s view, the celestial spheres and the terrestrial sphere were governed by different laws. In the celestial spheres, motion was eternal. In the terrestrial sphere, motion was temporary, always coming to an end without a mover of some sort. The celestial spheres were “perfect”, unchanging, whereas the terrestrial sphere was subject to decay. With the work of Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and ultimately, Newton, this was replaced by a world view in which the same fundamental laws governed heaven and earth. And these fundamental laws became precise, expressed using the language of mathematics, in particular the mathematics of infinitesimal changes, i.e., calculus. I cannot stress how fundamental this shift was to the development of modern science. Compared to this, the birth of quantum physics and the theory of relativity are… well, almost child’s play. Moving on, in the late 18th and the 19th century, another groundbreaking development took place: the advent of the “action principle”, the idea that the equations that govern a physical system can be derived by minimizing the “action”, a mathematical expression that characterizes a system’s evolution over time. It is difficult to stress just how critical the action principle has become in nearly all branches of fundamental physics: It governs mechanical systems, both particles and continua; classical field theories (electromagnetism and gravitation); and it forms an absolutely crucial foundation for the quantum theory. And no, physics did not come to an end in the 1930s. What was yet to happen was the development of quantum field theory, including non-Abelian theories, the modern understanding of the role intrinsic symmetries play in the behavior of quantum fields, ultimately leading to the development of the Standard Model of particle physics, a model that (as far as we know) accurately describes all the fundamental building blocks of the universe excluding gravitation. So yes, the first third of the 20th century was a remarkable period in physics, when two major revolutions took place at the same time. But that does not mean that similar, profound shifts in our understanding have not taken place before or after. And not just in physics; how about, for instance, biology, the understanding of DNA and the molecular foundations of genetics, that took place in the 1950s? It is perhaps true that fundamental physics has been a bit “stuck” in the past 50 years, not so much for lack of ideas but for lack of experimental evidence: Without hints from Nature, we can’t tell which approach, e.g., makes better sense as we try to improve the compatibility of the quantum theory and gravitation. Even so, look at the application side of things. It wasn’t that long ago that things like a blue LED seemed like unachievable “holy grails” in semiconductor technology, yet here we are, chances are you are reading this on a device with an OLED display, sitting in a room lit by a high power white LED lightbulb. Or not. Maybe you are not reading my silly words at all, consulting instead with a large language model, a culmination of some 70 years of research that began with simple “neural networks” designed to simulate the basic structure of neurons in the animal brain? So breakthroughs happen all the time. The first 30-odd years of the 20th century must have been an amazing time to be alive for a physicist, but you know what, I much rather do physics in 2024, with all the knowledge we have since added in the intervening century. Why is graviton difficult to detect? Do we have any good reasons to believe it exits in the first place? The graviton is difficult to detect because gravity is very weak, which means that the probability of any particular graviton to interact with matter is very, very, very low. The late Freeman Dyson in his 2012 Poincaré Prize lecture calculated that the Sun, in addition to the humongous amount of thermal energy it emits as electromagnetic radiation (mostly light), also emits about 79 megawatts of thermal gravitational radiation. Now 79 megawatts is not a lot for a star, but it is certainly a respectable amount: For comparison, we’ve been able to reliably detect a mere 8 watts in the form of a radio signal from the Pioneer 10 spacecraft when it was roughly 80 times farther from the Earth than the Sun. So Dyson calculated what it would take to detect a single graviton event, i.e., an atomic transition caused by a captured graviton, from this radiation, using the entire Earth as a perfect graviton detector. His result: We’d see roughly one graviton every billion years. That is how weakly gravity interacts with matter. Concerning the second half of the question, no, we do not “believe” that gravitons exist. Belief is done in other places. Rather, we know that if the gravitational field is a quantum field much like electromagnetism, in the so-called perturbative limit (basically, when the field is weak) it would manifest itself in the form of discrete quanta, which we call gravitons. So detecting gravitons would confirm our suspicion that gravitation, too, is a quantum phenomenon. Conversely, if we had a firm prediction that gravitons should be detected in a given experiment, and we failed to see those gravitons, that would at the very least falsify the idea that gravity is similar a a quantum field theory to electromagnetism. (Perhaps it is still a quantum theory, but something manifestly different.) The trouble is, we can do neither. We can neither detect gravitons nor reliably exclude their existence based on observations that we can do. So we end up speculating. There are plenty of theories out there, both quantum theories of gravitation and alternatives. Some are better than others, but we really have no way to decide which is right: without experiment, without observation, we are blind, and although we are reasonably clever monkeys, at no time in the history of science were we able to figure out something like this on our own, without hints from Nature as far as I know. Can you explain why the pressure inside of a black hole becomes infinite? The interior solution describing a collapsing astrophysical object turns out to be the same set of equations that would describe a collapsing cosmos. A hapless observer who found himself falling into a black hole, after crossing the event horizon, would find himself in such a collapsing “mini-Universe”. Depending on the size of this mini-Universe (determined by the amount of matter that fell, and will ever fall, into it), it may take anywhere from a millisecond to many hours, but the mini-Universe collapses. The observer would not live to see this, as ever increasing tidal forces would rip his body apart before the end. But that end (at least for a spherically symmetric black hole) inevitably happens: the famed “singularity” is not some bad spot that you can bypass by clever maneuvering, but a future moment in time at which (insofar as this mini-Universe is concerned) time itself comes to an end. So it’s not so much that pressure, density, etc., become infinite at this moment but rather, this moment literally is not part of existence: Whatever is inside the mini-Universe ceases to exist at this point. For outside observers, however, none of this ever happens. Even the event horizon itself remains forever in their future. Only by falling through it can the event horizon be experienced. That is the “classical” picture anyway. If we account for quantum physics, the answer is, we don’t really know what happens. In the absence of a quantum gravity theory, we can only take educated guesses, invoking what is known as the “semiclassical approximation”. One possibility (if you asked me, I think it’s the most likely one) is that the collapse never even happens as the black hole evaporates before its event horizon forms. In which case, there is no “inside” at all. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

How do scientists detect dark matter if it does not interact with light or other forms of matter except through gravity? How is it possible to observe something that does not emit light? To date, dark matter has not been detected. Its existence is inferred from the gravitational behavior of visible structures, but it has not been confirmed by direct detection, despite numerous attempts to do do. These failures do not mean that dark matter doesn’t exist, but they did exclude several plausible theoretical models. Meanwhile, precisely because dark matter’s existence has not yet been directly confirmed, the door remains open to viable alternatives, in the form of modified theories of gravitation that do away with the need for dark matter in the first place. However, this is not as easy as it sounds. The “dark matter paradigm” fits the data reasonably well. Modifying the theory of gravitation comes with unexpected consequences. Einstein’s theory works at very high precision here in the solar system; a modified theory of gravitation would have to reproduce these results. Dark matter does a decent job at producing data consistent with the large-scale structure formation (gravitational “clumping”) of matter; most theories of gravitation run into trouble. LIGO observations confirm that gravitational waves and light travel at the same speed; many modified gravity theories would predict something different and are therefore excluded. And the dark matter model accurately reproduces the statistical fluctuations of the cosmic microwave background, another difficult challenge for modified gravity. That is not to say that the standard dark matter model does not have its own share of difficulties, ranging from the famous Hubble tension (different values for the Hubble parameter when measured “locally” vs. inferred from cosmological observations) to the unexplained emergence of mature early galaxies and supermassive black holes in the early universe. So I daresay the jury is still out. We shall see what happens; dark matter is probably a safe horse to bet on, but its victory is by no means assured. Does quantum mechanics contradict determinism? Quantum mechanics says nothing about determinism. In its canonical form, by way of Schrödinger’s equation, it simply tells you how a particular mathematical entity, namely the wavefunction, representing the state of the system, evolves. Interpretations of quantum mechanics, on the other hand, are a different story. The most popular “Copenhagen” interpretation of quantum mechanics treats the wavefunction as a probability amplitude. The interpretation introduces the concept of a “measurement” (an act that is not described by quantum mechanics itself) that replaces the state of the system with an “eigenstate”, one of the many possible outcomes of that measurement. The wavefunction can be used to compute the probabilities associated with the various outcomes. If this “collapse of the wavefunction” really happens (so-called “objective collapse”) that would make the physics nondeterministic. The present state of the system only determines the probabilities of the various possible outcomes of the measurement. But before we conclude that “objective collapse” is the way to go, I’d advise caution. This whole “collapse” business is introduced for reasons that are philosophical, not physical. What the physics (the math, actually) tells us is a different story. The full present state of the system is not knowable on the basis of classical observables. Quantities that characterize the present state cannot be localized in space or time. This implies that some of these “hidden” properties of the system may, in fact, be constrained by future events. Seemingly paradoxically, this does not actually violate causality: Despite being fundamentally nonlocal, the quantum theory (at least in the form of quantum field theory) cannot be used to send signals from the future to the past. Nonetheless, this nonlocal business is disturbing. It is resolved if we assume that no, the future does not constrain the present, rather, the actual future happens because the act of measurement causes the system to collapse! (Again, objective collapse.) Unfortunately, that seems like a cure that is worse than the disease: This collapse has to happen simultaneously in the entire universe (after all, we replace one nonlocal description of the state of the system with a different one) including not just all locations but all times! OK, so what if we don’t go so far? Sure, “collapse” is a useful concept to deal with practical scenarios, e.g., when the instrument is obviously a macroscopic object (say, a cat) and its state is really never in doubt (no one has ever seen, or will ever see, a cat that is both alive and dead.) But then we have an important point to ponder: Sure, we use “collapse” as a practical tool, but we know that in reality, things really never collapse, and the wavefunction simply evolves towards a near-eigenstate because it is constrained by a future measurement. In other words, we’d be taking the nonlocality of quantum physics literally. In this case, we have a theory that is deterministic but nonlocal. Yet, in the form of quantum field theory, it would still be a theory that respects causality, with no faster-than-light or backwards-in-time influences, ever. I’m personally in favor of this viewpoint so my immediate reaction to the question is that yes, quantum physics is deterministic. I recognize though that there are many other popular interpretations, but in the end, all this interpretation business is firmly in the realm of philosophy, not physics: The equations are the same, the predictions are the same, the results of experiments are the same no matter what philosophical baggage we attach to them, mostly just to resolve the cognitive dissonance that the weirdness of the quantum world can produce in our minds. Which one is more dangerous, antimatter or black holes? Dangerous in what sense? I mean, look. Water is dangerous. You fall off a bridge into an icy river, you die. You fall off a ship in the middle of the ocean, you die. Oxygen is dangerous. It corrodes just about anything and everything, in some cases rather explosively. One careless act inside a wood frame house and you die a horrible, fiery death. Cats are dangerous. These cuddly little guys can give you scratches, can bite you, cause a wound to be infected, and if you’re not careful, you might even die. They can also carry rabies. Antimatter? Take a banana. It is slightly radioactive because it contains the naturally occurring radioactive isotope, potassium-40. These atoms decay, and rarely, maybe once in 100,000 decaying atoms, the decay produces a positron: the antimatter partner of the electron. Is it possible for an object to become heavier than anything else in existence, including black holes, if it reaches lightspeed through acceleration? Objects do not become heavier by acceleration. Objects gain kinetic energy by acceleration, as measured in the reference frame of other objects that do not accelerate along with the object in question. Decades ago, relativity texts often introduced the concept of “relativistic mass”, which lumped together the (intrinsic) rest mass of the moving object with its (observer-dependent) kinetic energy. Fortunately, this concept is not much used anymore and, well, good riddance, because it led to a lot of misunderstandings. So no, an object will not become heavier no matter how close to the vacuum speed of light it moves in some observer’s reference frame. (Keep in mind that motion is always relative: objects move relative to other objects, in their own reference frames they are always at rest.) Is it true that everything travels at a constant velocity in deep space, near the speed of light? No, it is not true. First of all, in the context of relativity theory, it is important to remember that the concept of speed is relative. Things do not travel at some velocity, nor do that stay put. Things travel relative to other things. To give you an example that dates back to Galileo: Suppose you are on a sailing ship, sitting in a windowless cabin as the ship sails on perfectly smooth seas. You are staring at a glass on the table in front of you. The glass is not moving. Or is it? How could you even tell? Relative to you, the glass is at rest. Relative to the shore, it moves at some velocity (how fast do medieval sailing ships move anyway?) along with you and the table and the rest of the ship. But relative to the Sun? It moves about 30 kilometers every second! Or how about relative to the central region of the Milky Way? We’re now up to roughly 200 km/s. And then relative to some really distant objects in deep space, you, your glass and the table it sits own, your ship, the Earth, the Sun, the Milky Way all move at a speed close to the vacuum speed of light. And it goes both ways. From your perspective, it’s not you or the Earth that is moving so fast, but the distant galaxy! However, if there are aliens on that galaxy, they’d say it’s you who is moving and they’re the ones standing still. So as I said, motion is relative. And constant it is not. If there were no forces (including gravity) acting on objects, motion (relative as it is) would always be in a straight line at constant velocity. But there are forces. Gravity in particular (a force that we often interpret geometrically) alters the trajectories of objects. So they no longer move in a straight line or at a constant speed relative to other things. The Earth moves around the Sun, and its Sun-relative velocity changes in magnitude, too, as its orbit is elliptical. The velocity of the Earth relative to, say, Mars, is even more twisted. These specific examples notwithstanding if there is one thing that is worth remembering, it’s that velocity is always relative. That applies even to light in a vacuum. The magnitude of its velocity is the same for all observers, but the direction in which a light ray travels is different in different observer reference frames. (In fact, if you look up the concept of aberration in astronomy, this has been known since before relativity theory, for over 300 years as a matter of fact).

What makes the Schwarzschild metric the simplest solution to Einstein's equations? Nothing. The Schwarzschild solution is not the simplest solution to Einstein’s field equations. The simplest solution is Minkowski spacetime, representing empty space. In the usual coordinate representation, it is simply g μ ν = d i a g ( 1 , − 1 , − 1 , − 1 ) . Okay, okay, I get it, you are wondering about the simplest nontrivial solution. How do we find solutions that are simple? In general, the Einstein field equations represent a set of ten coupled second-order differential equations. We can eliminate four by choosing coordinates appropriately, but that still leaves six. But then… how about assuming some symmetry? For instance, let’s make the system spherically symmetric. That means that the solution depends only on the distance from some point of origin, not on direction. There, two more degrees of freedom gone. Oh, and let’s make the solution static, so it does not depend on time either; That’s one more degree of freedom. And then, how about… Well, let’s make it a vacuum solution! Now there is no dependence on energy density or (isotropic) pressure either. This allows us to write down the metric using spherical coordinates ( t , r , θ , ϕ ) as g μ ν = d i a g ( B ( r ) , − A ( r ) , − r 2 , − r 2 sin 2 θ ) , ultimately yielding only two differential equations, one of which is trivially solvable: A ′ r + A 2 − A = 0 is solved by A = r / ( r − C 1 ) where C 1 is an integration constant; after this, we find that B = C 2 / A with C 2 another constant. Reconciling this in the nonrelativistic approximation with Newton’s theory tells us that C 1 = 2 G M / c 2 , C 2 = 1 , where M is the mass of a compact source of gravitation. This is not the only “simplest” nontrivial solution, by the way. Another solution, almost as simple as this one, assumes the presence of matter, specifically matter in the form of a homogeneous (same everywhere) “isotropic perfect fluid” (a medium characterized by isotropic pressure, no sheer, no viscosity). Unlike the Schwarzschild metric, which depends only on the radial coordinate, this new solution depends only on the time coordinate: it will be in the form of the Friedmann equations of cosmology. And interestingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, when we consider actual astrophysical collapse of a spherically symmetric cloud of dust, as the collapse approaches its asymptotic end state, the exterior will be characterized by the Schwarzschild solution, whereas the interior will be described by the Friedmann equations characterizing a collapsing mini-universe. More complex solutions may be obtained by relaxing the symmetry conditions. The next step up the ladder, so to speak, is to let go of spherical symmetry, replacing it with axial symmetry, which leads to the rotating Kerr solution. What if when your at the singularity of a black hole (if there is one), looking back out to space may look like a singularity also? Can that be? Ok-kay… when you are “at the singularity” of a black hole, your world has come to an end. The singularity is not a place you can be at, but a time: specifically, for anything unfortunate enough to have crossed the event horizon of a (Schwarzschild) black hole, it is an unavoidable moment in time in the near future. In case you are wondering what you might see after you crossed the event horizon but before your world ends at the singularity: no, you cannot “look back”. Not without a time machine. Like the singularity, the event horizon is also a moment in time: a moment in time in your past now. Your present is characterized by an environment that can be mathematically described by the same equations as a collapsing mini-universe. (You may not be a “comoving observer” so the mini-universe might have a skewed appearance, so to speak, but that makes no real difference.) This mini-universe is collapsing and there’s nothing you can do about it, just as there’s nothing you can do, here and now, tou avoid encountering 8 AM tomorrow a few hours from now. So no, you cannot look back. Now whether or not it is even possible to reach an event horizon or if it perhaps evaporates first, or whether or not a black hole with even a small amount of rotation might look materially different “inside” from the Schwarzschild case… I don’t know, and I don’t think anyone has an unambiguous answer, since Hawking evaporation remains a semiclassical model, and as for spinning black holes, no one constructed yet a fully convincing model of what a collapsing, spinning cloud of matter does beyond the horizon. But we do know how things work in the case of a non-spinning Schwarzschild black hole: There is no looking back. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is Newton's conception of gravity as incompatible with Einstein's concept of gravity, as Einstein's is from the quantum? How, or how not? None of the above incompatibilities are true. First, Newton himself knew that his gravitational theory is incomplete. It involved “action at a distance” between celestial bodies, with no means, no medium to mediate that interaction. To quote the man himself (letter to Bentley, Feb 25, 1692/93): "That gravity should be innate inherent & {essential} to matter so that one body may act upon another at a distance through a vacuum without the mediation of any thing else by & through which their action or force {may} be conveyed from one to another is to me so great an absurdity that I beleive no man who has in philosophical matters any competent faculty of thinking can ever fall into it. Gravity must be caused by an agent {acting} consta{ntl}y according to certain laws, but whether this agent be material or immaterial is a question I have left to the consideration of my readers." Einstein completed this theory, though by no means was he the first to try. In the wake of the success of Maxwell’s theory, especially after special relativity made it clear that the electromagnetic field is a fundamental entity, not just waves of some medium (the luminiferous aether), many sought a similar field theory of gravitation. It took a while to understand why a scalar theory would not work, and why a tensor theory necessarily doubles as the observed geometry of spacetime. Einstein succeeded, and by doing so, ultimately answered the riddle posed by Newton more than two centuries earlier. And of course Einstein’s theory yields precisely Newton’s in the weak field, nonrelativistic limit. General relativity is a classical field theory. It is not fundamentally incompatible with quantum physics. We can do quantum field theory on the curved background of general relativity. (Indeed, popular topics such as Hawking radiation arise precisely as a result of such an approach). We can even have quantum matter act as the source of classical gravitation, in the form of semiclassical gravity. We find this unsatisfactory, however, in much the same way Newton was not satisfied with his own theory of gravitation: We sense that it is not the final word on the subject and further improvements are needed. But we would expect such an improved theory to yield Einstein’s in the semiclassical limit, and yield Newton’s in the semiclassical, nonrelativistic limit. No incompatibilities there, just gradual improvements in our understanding, one step at a time. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If space is expanding (or perhaps 'stretching' is a better verb) at a rate we call the Hubble Constant (or thereabouts), at what rate is time expanding (in seconds per kilometer per petasecond - s/km/Ps)? You stumbled upon one of the silliest, most persistent misunderstandings concerning cosmology. No, space is not expanding. Nor is it contracting or dancing the tango. Or perhaps it does… if it did, we would not know. Space does not have little markers attached to it by which it could be measured. Space is not a physical entity that would carry energy or momentum. In short, space is not a thing. But, but… cosmic expansion! The Friedmann equations! The Hubble-parameter! Well… the famous Friedmann equations, which also define the Hubble parameter, represent a specific application of Einstein’s field equations, for the case of a cosmos that is filled with matter such that the distribution is homogeneous in space (i.e., uniform density) and isotropic (no preferred direction). But… Einstein’s field equations! It’s all about the bending of space and time! Er… Not really. There are two things in Einstein’s field equations: The gravitational field, represented by a so-called tensor quantity, and the energy-momentum of matter, also represented by a tensor quantity. It is true that Einstein’s field equations can be interpreted geometrically. So what? We can also interpret electromagnetism using geometry (just ask Weyl, or consider how the electromagnetic interaction is introduced through a covariant derivative in quantum electrodynamics.) What makes gravity special is that matter is introduced into the equations solely through its energy-momentum; what the stuff is made of makes no difference. This, namely the so-called weak equivalence principle, implies that the geometry we see is the only geometry that can be measured. In contrast, in the case of electromagnetism the geometry that we see depends on the charge-to-mass ratio of the object used to measure it, so there is no one-and-only, unique geometry. (I shall refrain from quoting Einstein himself again, as I’ve already done so many times in the past here on Quora, arguing against taking the geometric interpretation, which he called a mental aid, too literally, too dogmatically.) Anyhow, back to cosmology. What those Friedmann equations tell us is how the gravitational field changes on the one hand, and how the density of matter changes at the same time. If we think of matter as particles, that implies that the characteristic distance between particles changes over time. This characteristic distance can also be thought of as part of geometry, thus characterize the gravitational field itself. But, I stress, the geometry part is interpretation. The actual, physical things in the equation are matter and the gravitational field. In the standard form in which the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric (i.e., the gravitational field) is written, we have d s 2 = c 2 d t 2 − a ( t ) 2 d R 2 , where a ( t ) is the time-dependent “scale factor”. When it is applied to a universe dominated by matter with little or no pressure (that is, ordinary nonrelativistic matter, or also “cold dark matter”) that a ( t ) indeed serves well as the measure by which the typical distance between particle changes over time. Note that time itself does not have a factor like that. And a ( t ) ceases to be a valid measure of this change of density if the matter in question is not predominantly “pressureless dust”. Which, incidentally, is already the case today, as (at least according to the prevailing ΛCDM cosmological model) about 70% of matter in the present universe is “dark energy”, stuff with large negative pressure, the density of which remains constant over time. But putting all that aside: In terms of actual, observable effects, what we see of course is that light from distant objects is shifted in frequency. For objects relatively close to our Milky Way galaxy, this shift in frequency is mainly a velocity-induced Doppler frequency shift, as those objects are receding from us (or we, from them). But for objects that are very far from here, high-redshift objects, the dominant contribution to the redshift is gravitational, which can be thought of as a result of changing gravitational time dilation as the average gravitational field in the distant past (when matter was more dense) was greater than it is today. As to the Hubble parameter, it kind of captures both effects (it is defined as H = ˙ a / a where the dot represents differentiation with respect to time) but keep in mind that it is not really a constant at all; as its definition itself implies, since a ( t ) is a function of time, so is H ( t ) . I know, I know, this is not the kind of simple, concise answer that you might have hoped for. But I am trying to follow Einstein’s advice: Make things as simple as possible but no simpler. Relativistic cosmology may not be the most complicated subject in modern physics, but that does not mean it is easy to grasp or always intuitive. Why does a particle wave exist, and is there a way to comprehend it? I presume this question is about quantum mechanics. In the classical world, we’re used to things working, well, normally. Take a flying cannonball. At any given moment in time, we can describe its position x and we can describe its velocity, or rather, its momentum p (same thing as velocity, for all practical intents and purposes.) The quantities x and p are numbers (maybe sets of numbers, i.e., coordinates or coordinate components, but expressed using numbers nonetheless.) Because they are numbers, we can multiply them in any order: the products p ⋅ x and x ⋅ p represent the same thing. This all makes perfectly good sense, but Nature has this nasty habit of not obeying our expectations when it comes to what we think makes good sense and what does not. As it turns out, things in Nature do not obey this simple arithmetic. Particles are not acting like miniature cannonballs. They do not have positions and momenta. They have states. And to the extent that they exhibit properties that can be interpreted, viewed, measured as positions or momenta under the right circumstances, these can be represented in mathematics by so-called operators like ^ x or ^ p , acting on a state ψ . And these operators do not obey the (commutative) rule of multiplication: ^ p ⋅ ^ x ≠ ^ x ⋅ ^ p . This is the essence of quantum physics. And this has two consequences. First, that state of the quantum system, ψ . It is governed by the famous Schrödinger equation. That equation is a “wave equation”, which is to say, under most circumstances it will give some kind of a periodic solution. So the state of this quantum system will have wave-like behavior, which includes, e.g., constructive and destructive interference, something cannonballs never do. Second, those operators I mentioned, for positions and momenta: Under the right circumstances they yield measurable numbers. So with the right experiment, that quantum system still exhibits behavior that makes it appear like a miniature cannonball. So when you fire, say, an electron, while the electron is en route it does not have a position of a momentum in the classical sense. Its existence is described by the state ψ , its wavefunction. But when it impacts, say, the fluorescent screen of a CRT, that interaction confines it to a well-defined position. Its position operator ^ x , acting on its state, produces a set of coordinates, the location where you see a flash on the screen. If this explanation appears a little abstract, a little hard to make sense of, that is no accident. Quantum physics cannot be intuited. To use a stupid analogy, almost all of us had a chance to play with language models like ChatGPT in the past year or so. Ignoring their more recent attempts to integrate language and visual capabilities, the original language model has no visual experiences. No ability to intuit or visualize anything related to space or geometry. It can still reason about these things, but often it struggles, as its words are not connected to any experience that it would have at its disposal. We humans are in the same situation with quantum physics. Just as language models have no visual cortex, our brains lack a “quantum physics cortex” that would allow us to intuit the quantum world. Therefore, like the language models, we have to resort to painful, slow, step-by-step reasoning, relying on the reasonably precise language of mathematics. However painful this feels, it is important to remember that any attempt to visualize quantum physics using our intuition that is rooted in classical physics is not only doomed to fail, it will likely become an obstacle to understanding. Can Hawking radiation (absorption of mass by a hypothetical particle and destruction of mass by a star) occur in a neutron star? Is it possible or not and why? The answer is yes, and I can explain why both using simple reasoning and the math. On the simple reasoning side: If a black hole radiates Hawking radiation in the present, it cannot be because it’s a black hole as the black hole has not formed yet. The particles collapsing into a black hole take forever (as seen by outside observers) to reach the limit when they’d form an event horizon. This is the essence, e.g., of the famous Oppenheimer-Snyder paper that, in 1939, described for the first time this process of “continued contraction”. This also means that, at least in principle, the particles may interact with one another in the last minute, second, picosecond before forming a horizon (as measured in their own reference frame) and turn around; we can never be 100% certain that this won’t happen as the black hole has not formed yet! So perhaps it never will… yet there is Hawking radiation. But never mind the fairy tale. I hold in my hand a paper, well, a single sheet of paper really as Hawking’s paper really is short: It’s his 1974 publication in Nature, titled “Black hole explosions?” Let me quote two key sentences from this paper: “The β i j will not be zero because the time dependence of the metric during the collapse will cause a certain amount of mixing of positive and negative frequencies. […] The number of particles created and emitted to infinity in a gravitational collapse can therefore be determined by calculating the coefficients β i j . ” In short: What is needed for Hawking-radiation is not a horizon but a time asymmetry; specifically, the asymmetry due to collapse, as a result of which the past and the future are not identical. What this tells us is that any collapsing cloud of matter will emit Hawking radiation unless the collapse is halted by some interaction and the configuration becomes static. In the case of a black hole, the collapse never ends. In other cases, it may. But so long as the collapse is in-progress, Hawking radiation follows, according to Hawking’s own reasoning. Mass and energy are equivalent. Heavy masses dilate time. Could enough energy in a closed container dilate time? If not, why not? I have a feeling reading this question that it was inspired by some kind of (unfortunately fairly common) magical misunderstanding of “energy”. What do you think “energy” is? Is it something that we can scoop out of a container with a ladle? Use it to fill another container to the brim? Not really. By and large, energy can be two things: Potential energy or kinetic energy. Potential energy is associated with how things interact with each other, attracting or repulsing one another. This is the ability to do work: The ability to bring things into motion. Kinetic energy, in turn, is the energy associated with the motion itself. So then, going back to the question: To put “energy” in the box, we need to put things into the box: things that interact (with each other or even with themselves), things that move. And all these things will add to the energy-content of the box. As per the mass-energy equivalence relationship, it means that the box will have more inertia. More mass, in other words. and yes, that also means more gravity. But then, let me get to the second part of the question. Heavy masses dilate time? Not exactly. I know, we say that, I probably said that a few times, lazy language and all, but let’s keep in mind that the theory is called the theory of relativity for a reason: it’s not about what happens to time, it’s about what, for instance, two clocks measure that follow different worldlines between the same two events. I.e., how the two clocks behave relative to one another. And yes, by and large, clocks that spend more time in a gravitational field tend to count fewer ticks, but that’s because their worldlines are, in an abstract sense, “shorter”, not because of anything that might have happened either to the clocks or to time itself. So yes, a heavy box with plenty of energy-content will have more gravity, and as a result, clocks following worldlines that pass near the box may count fewer ticks. As to why that box is heavy, it doesn’t matter. Heavy always means more energy-content. Whether that energy content exists because we put lead in the box, or because we lined the inside of the box with perfect mirrors and then let in a tremendous quantity of light, never to escape… no difference. What matters, as I said, is the energy-content. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can a black hole at its center be destroyed? If so, what would be the method to do so? Would the intense gravity make it impossible to escape and cause any damage? Let me describe to you an imaginary journey into a classical black hole. ("Classical" in the sense that I am ignoring quantum effects, notably Hawking radiation, which might even prevent the black hole from forming in the first place. So let's say that you are not only in a very good spaceship, but you are also almost imprevious to extreme acceleration and extreme tidal forces. You hope into your spaceship, travel to the nearest collapsing sphere of matter that will ultimately form a black hole, and choose a trajectory that will end up in the black hole as well. If the collapsing matter has negligible pressure, its collapse will not be slowed down by any means. Yet to those on the outside, the process of the collapse will appear to slow as the cloud gets close to becoming a black hole. That is because of extreme gravitational time dilation: anything that happens near this collapsing cloud of matter will appear in slow motion to anyone far away. Not to you though. You will find that you will approach the surface of this collapsing cloud, but you won't quite be able to catch up with it. Meanwhile, however, as the gravitational field gets stronger, you will notice that what was a spherical surface below now appears to "curl up" on the sides. That is because of the gravitational deflection of light: many light rays that start off going upward will be bent downward, so they will appear to hit your eyeball from above! What was one a surface below begins to form a wall around you, and soon enough, it will feel like you are in a vertical tunnel, or well, its opening rapidly closing above you. Suppose you chicken out at the very last split second, punch a button, and with your Extremely Powerful Rocket [tm] you escape. Much to your surprise, you'll find that what has taken only a few seconds by your reckoning took a year outside. Or a thousand years. Or a quintillion years. This is why those on the outside can never be sure that the black hole even forms; no matter how long they wait, there's a chance that you re-emerge. It's only a question of how close you cut it before punching out. But what if you don't? Well, there will be a moment when the matter above your head closes up. There is no opening anymore. No walls really, either, as this is also the moment when you caught up with all the collapsing matter after all, so now you are inside the cloud. Inside a homogeneous (same everywhere) isotropic (no preferred direction) cloud of matter that forms a collapsing mini-universe, in which you are trapped. The moment when this happened is the event horizon. NOT a place. Not a location to which you can return. A moment — now a moment in the past — of time. So without a time machine, you are doomed. This mini-universe is a collapsing universe, the exact opposite of the kind of universe we seem to live in, outside of the black hole. Second by second, minute by minute it becomes denser. (Or millisecond by millisecond, if the collapsing cloud weighed "only" as much as, say, three times the mass of our Sun, or a million times the mass of the Earth.) Did I say same everywhere? Yes, I did. I meant it. There is no center, no edge of this cloud. This entire self-enclosed mini-universe is filled with matter everywhere. And you have very little time left. And perhaps that's when you recall something that you may have heard before in the past: The so-called "singularity" is not some center either. Rather, it is the moment in time when density, pressure, temperature, etc., everything in this mini-universe diverges, becomes infinite. The mini-universe ceases to exist (it's called geodesic incompleteness). Along with you, of course. Think this scenario through and now contemplate if it is even meaningful to talk about "destroying" a black hole. What exactly would that "destruction" do? Remember, to those on the outside, the black hole does not even exist yet, no matter how long they wait. Whereas for those on the inside, the black hole is the ONLY thing that exists, and its fate is sealed: soon enough everything, including time itself (!) comes to an end in this doomed mini-universe.

Why is our universe considered flat with angles of a triangle adding to 180 degrees, when clearly spacetime is curved as gravity, intrinsic curvature where the angles do not add to180 degrees? Do not confuse spatial curvature with spacetime curvature. The geometry of spacetime involves, well, both space and time (d’uh!) Newtonian gravity maps into the time part. Contrary to stylish but ultimately grossly misleading imagery that often accompanies popular science articles introducing gravity and relativity theory, Newtonian gravity is not about bending space. It is primarily about changing the rate at which clocks tick. This can be measured. E.g., an atomic clock at the top of a tall building ticks noticeably faster than the same clock at the ground floor. (And yes, it is also accounted for in GPS navigation, for instance.) In contrast, spatial curvature here on the surface of the Earth contributes no more than a few parts per billion compared to the Newtonian part. Now this is spatial curvature in the presence of a gravitating body, such as the Earth. When we talk about the universe, we’re not talking about local gravitational fields, but large, cosmic scales. We know that the universe expands (plenty of evidence supporting that conclusion), and we know, therefore, that the average gravitational field changes over time. That is the reason for cosmological redshift: When we look at very distant objects, much of the redshift that we see is due not to the fact that they are receding from us (they do), but due to gravitational time dilation, i.e., the rate at which clocks tick now vs. the rate at which they ticked back then. But the question is, what about space? Is there noticeable spatial curvature on cosmic scales? We see no evidence of that. In fact, every indication is that the universe, on average, is spatially flat. Now the equations tell us that if the universe is close to being spatially flat today, it had to be astonishingly close to being spatially flat in the distant past, because spatial curvature increases over time. Something astonishingly close to zero just does not sit well in a fundamental theory. So the prevailing assumption is that no, it’s not astonishingly close to zero; it is zero, or at least, we assume that it is zero until and unless see evidence to the contrary. Debroglie says wavelength is inversely proportional to velocity. But velocity is relative, and it is 0 in that particle’s resting frame of reference. So what does it mean for a particle to have infinite wavelength? Well, if you think of the de Broglie wavelength as a means to characterize how a particle moves, in the reference frame in which the particle is at rest, infinite wavelength (zero frequency) simply means that the particle is not moving. I know, it sounds kind of tautological, but that’s what it boils down to: no movement, no wave, zero frequency, hence infinite wavelength. Of course keep in mind that we’re not talking about a physical wave here. The wavelength here is simply a mathematical characterization of the amplitude of the particle’s wavefunction, which determines the probability density of finding the particle in a given state. Zero momentum means that the particle is not moving, but it can be with equal probability anywhere. This also follows from the uncertainty principle, since precise determination of a particle’s momentum means its position is completely indeterminate. Einstein believed quantum mechanics wasn’t fundamental and there must be a deeper theory. Was he correct? Well… yes and no, but context is all-important here. Einstein passed away in 1955. At the time, modern quantum field theory was still in its infancy. Yang-Mills theory that proved fundamental to the development of the Standard Model was just a few months old. In any case, I doubt Einstein had more than a very superficial familiarity with then-recent developments. The quantum mechanics that he was familiar with was basically quantum particle theory, characterized by the Schrödinger equation or maybe the relativistic Dirac equation, which were predominantly interpreted in accordance with the Copenhagen school as equations that yield a probability amplitude. Quite clearly, Einstein was not comfortable with physics that yielded only probabilities. Moreover, the Copenhagen interpretation assigns a role to the “observer”, which is fundamentally at odds with a world view in which Nature does what it does, regardless of whether it is observed or not by a human, a cat, or some instrument. So what do we know that Einstein didn’t? For starters, modern quantum field theory and the Standard Model of particle physics. Then there’s also Bell’s theorem that demonstrates that quantum physics is essentially nonlocal, which is to say, the behavior of the system is governed, in part, by constraints that cannot be nailed down to any specific location in space or moment in time. What it means, in practice, is that the state of a quantum system is constrained not just by the past and the present but also by the future, yet the physics remains causal in the sense that rearranging something in the future has no observable consequences on the past (sorry, no quantum time machines). In light of this, the probabilistic interpretation gains a new meaning: ignore the future constraint and the system becomes underdetermined. Instead of telling us what the future will be, the (underdetermined) wavefunction now indeed just yields probabilities. When the future becomes the present, and the outcome of an experiment becomes known, the probability becomes a certainty and we can replace the old wavefunction with a new one (“wavefunction collapse”) in our description of the system. Would this have made Einstein more comfortable? I don’t know. But I do believe that this is markedly different from the quantum physics Einstein knew. Which implies that yes, he was right to criticize quantum mechanics and, in particular, its Copenhagen interpretation. As a local theory, quantum mechanics is necessarily incomplete (again, I am alluding to Bell’s theorem here) and leads to the unsatisfying probabilistic Copenhagen interpretation. But what we got in exchange is, in some ways, even weirder. Yes, quantum field theory has spectacular successes. It can do what quantum mechanics could not ever do, model how particles are created and destroyed. It is also robustly causal and relativistic. But it is just as nonlocal as quantum physics has ever been, and with Bell’s theorem, we know that this nonlocality is not going to go away. Then there’s the problem of renormalizability: We have no renormalizable quantum field theory of gravitation. To many, it seems to imply that the Standard Model (and by extension, quantum field theory as a whole) is just a useful “effective” theory, which will fail at the Planck energy scale, to be replaced by something more fundamental that would unify particle physics with gravity in a more satisfactory way than, say, semiclassical gravity. But much of what I described here happened after Einstein’s death. The quantum theory that he was critical of was really not modern quantum field theory, but quantum particle physics, along with the probabilistic Copenhagen interpretation. I think his criticism of that school of thought was spot on. What was not spot on is his relentless attempt to construct a more fundamental classical theory, which consumed much of his time in the final decades of his life, but ultimately proved futile, little more than a half-forgotten footnote in the history of modern physics. (To anyone seriously interested in the subject, beyond the superb scientific biography of Einstein by Abraham Pais, I’d recommend the hard-to-find 1966 monograph, Einstein’s Unified Field Theory, by Marie-Antoinette Tonnelat.) How do we obtain covariant matrix from contravariant matrix? Is the product of contravariant metric tensor and covariant metric tensor equal to kronecker delta? Indeed, the inner product of the covariant and the contravariant forms of the metric yield the Kronecker-delta: g μ ν g ν κ = δ κ μ . Matrices are (or rather, can be) representations of tensors in a specific coordinate system. There is no such thing as a “covariant matrix” or a “contravariant matrix”. If we wanted to be absolutely pedantic about it, a covariant rank-2 tensor should be represented by a row of rows (i.e., a matrix of only one row, with its elements themselves row vectors) and a contravariant rank-2 tensor would be a column of columns; only a mixed-index tensor could be represented properly by a matrix of numbers. But we “cheat” and use matrices anyway for both covariant/contravariant and mixed-index tensors, dropping a bit of pedantic rigor for the sake of convenience. In any case, the general rule is that we use the metric to raise and lower indices, i.e., turn something covariant into something contravariant and vice versa. So to turn a contravariant rank-2 tensor into a covariant one, we’d need to multiply by the covariant metric tensor twice: A μ ν = g μ κ g ν λ A κ λ . So then, if we choose to forego pedantry and represent g μ ν and A κ λ as matrices g and A , it would amount to multiplying A by g on the left and the transpose of g on the right: A ′ = g ⋅ A ⋅ g T , where I used A ′ for the matrix representing A μ ν . Of course the metric is (usually) symmetric, so g = g T . If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Does the space bend like this: The closer to the center of the mass you are, the smaller it is, things tending to go where it is smaller, explaining gravity? No. What we experience as Newtonian gravity is primarily related to the rate of clocks. The stronger the gravitational field, the slower clocks tick in it compared to other clocks in deep space. This results in altered trajectories, objects falling onto, or orbiting, other objects. Spatial effects of relativity theory only begin to play a substantial role when either the gravitational field is very strong (neutron stars and beyond) or the particles probing the field move near the vacuum speed of light. In fact, this leads to Einstein’s famous prediction that particles of light, i.e., photons, will have trajectories near a mass that would be deflected by twice the amount one would calculate using Newtonian gravity alone. This prediction was first confirmed by Eddington’s famous expedition in 1919, observing a solar eclipse and the slight displacement, visible during the eclipse, of stars that appear in the sky near the Sun.
