What is the current understanding of dark energy using general relativity? Can GR provide any insights into the nature of this mysterious phenomenon in our universe? To answer this question, I must first point out a very important fact: General relativity is not a theory of matter. It is a theory of gravitation. Insofar as matter is concerned, general relativity simply states that matter “couples universally and minimally” to the gravitational field: in technical terms, this is written as T μ ν = − ( 2 / √ − g ) δ S m / δ g μ ν , which is a mathematical equation that essentially tells us that the stress-energy-momentum of matter serves as the source of the gravitational field. But as to what that matter is, on that subject general relativity remains silent. That is not to say that we cannot speculate about the nature of matter. In particular, we often postulate that matter, whatever it is made of, behaves on large scales as an “isotropic perfect fluid”: that is to say, a medium entirely characterized by its density and pressure. (There is no directionality, no stresses, no viscosity, just density and pressure). A perfect fluid is easily characterized then by the ratio of its pressure and its energy density. In any sensible system of units, these two quantities are measured using the same units. Energy is force time distance, volume is area times distance, therefore energy density: energy divided by volume, is the same as pressure: force divided by area. Which means that the ratio of these two quantities is a pure number, not dependent on the choice of units. This number is zero for stuff with no pressure (sometimes called “dust”). It’s very close to zero for most “normal” matter. For a relativistic gas (gas so hot, its particles move around at nearly the speed of light) the ratio is 1/3. But really, a perfect fluid makes sense with that ratio being anywhere between -1 (yes, negative pressure) and +1. (Less than -1 means an unstable cosmos, more than +1 means a medium in which sound travels faster than light.) The rest is easy, so to speak. When we look at astronomical observations on cosmological scales, we find that the data can be modeled using general relativity if the universe is made up of 30% “dust” and 70% stuff with the aforementioned ratio being -1. We call this perfect fluid “dark energy”. Of the 30% dust, about 4% is “normal” matter (not exactly dust, but close, as most normal matter is not relativistic). The rest is “dark matter”. We have no idea what “dark matter” and “dark energy” are, although there are many proposals. The only thing we know about them is that they are, well, “dark” although “transparent” might be closer to the truth: They do not interact with (emit, absorb, block or reflect) light, indeed they do not interact with matter at all (or if they do, they do so very, very weakly). That’s all we really know about this “dark” stuff. Everything else is conjecture, since none of this “dark” stuff has ever been observed. And it is of course still eminently possible that none of this “dark” stuff exists, but rather, our theories are on the wrong track. In any case, the answer, if it comes, won’t come from general relativity. It will either be in a form that modifies general relativity (and does away with the need for “dark” things) or in a form of a better theory of matter, hopefully one with directly testable predictions so that it can be validated by observation.

What we call gravitational acceleration (9.8ms2) is a phenomenon observable only by the observer on the ground due to the dilation of time, which passes more slowly for him, giving the impression that the object in free fall is accelerating? No, that is not the way it works. At the Newtonian level, gravitational acceleration is simply a result of a force, acting at a distance between any two objects. If one of the objects is the Earth and the other is, well, anything at or near the surface of the Earth, that object will accelerate towards the center of the Earth at approximately 9.8 meters per seconds squared. In general relativity, the corresponding Newtonian potential is ascribed to the spacetime metric, specifically the “time” part of the metric that determines the rate at which clocks tick. And indeed, in a gravitational field, clocks tick more slowly than far away from the gravitating object. But this difference is minuscule. It’s barely more than one part in a billion. Tiny, tiny, tiny. So no, gravitational acceleration is not some illusion that we see because of gravitational time dilation. It is a very real deviation from straight-line, constant velocity motion. How real? Well, drop something not too heavy (we don’t want any injuries here) on your foot to find out! However, the reason why this deviation exists, why objects accelerate toward each other, is much more subtle. When we write down the relativistic equations of motion, they represent trajectories in “spacetime”. Don’t let this phrase mislead you. It’s nothing mysterious. If you draw a simple plot, with, say, time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical, and use it to characterize the motion of something, you drew a plot in spacetime. The thing is, the path connecting an initial state and a final state for any trajectory will have certain geometric properties in general relativity. This causes the path to be “bent”, representing a trajectory with changing velocity, i.e., acceleration. Ultimately, this bending occurs because the “length” of a trajectory is not measured in the conventional way, but in a way prescribed by the theory (Riemannian geometry, actually). The actual calculation is not terribly difficult but it cannot be explained easily as there are mathematical prerequisites for the formulas to make sense (the concept of geodesics, connection coefficients, covariant derivatives, etc.) Long story short, time dilation is minuscule (around one part in a billion) but it’s enough to change trajectories to produce a very real (not illusionary) downward acceleration (9.8 meters per seconds squared here on the surface of the Earth) by altering the trajectories of free objects. Spacetime is curved by gravity. Can other fields also curve spacetime? Er, no. Spacetime is not curved by gravity. Don’t think of it that way. Rather, gravity is characterized by what is known as a tensor quantity. This tensor quantity “couples to matter universally and minimally”. These two words have specific meaning. “Universally” means that material properties make no difference: gravity couples to matter the same way, regardless of what that matter is made of. “Minimally” means that the coupling is geometric in nature: That is to say, it determines things like inner products between vectors, volume elements in integrals, etc. Putting the two together implies that gravity can be interpreted as a universal geometry, i.e., the geometry of spacetime. Do we have to interpret gravity this way? No, we don’t, and indeed, none other than Einstein himself warned against taking the geometric interpretation too literally. (There are at least two practical reasons: First, taking the geometric interpretation dogmatically prevents us from thinking about alternative theories that do not have these two properties; second, most sensible approaches toward a quantum theory of gravity start with treating gravity as a force, not as geometry.) Can other fields be like gravity? We can certainly contemplate other possibilities. But no other known field has these properties. Electromagnetism couples to charges, so the coupling depends on material properties, such as the charge-to-mass ratio, so it’s not universal, albeit it can be viewed as geometric (indeed, there were early attempts to lump together electromagnetism and gravity by way of geometry: Weyl’s linear vs. quadratic ground forms, or the five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein theory are examples.) The weak and the strong interactions are neither universal nor geometric, so no. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If a neutron star was made entirely of neutrons, would it eventually collapse into a black hole? No, a neutron star does not collapse into a black hole unless it is heavy enough to do so. In a neutron star, neutrons are pushed apart by what is known as neutron degeneracy pressure. It is a direct consequence of neutrons being fermions, subject to the Pauli exclusion principle: Two neutrons cannot be in the same quantum state. However, this degeneracy pressure is not infinite. When the mass of the neutron star reaches what is known as the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) limit, strange things start to happen. The reason why I am being vague is because at this point, the story becomes less certain. Neutrons, after all, are not elementary particles, but composites: They consist of triplets of quarks. When the TOV limit is reached, neutrons break down and… form what? If anything? As far as I know, no one ever calculated with certainty what happens at this point, but the general consensus is that once neutron degeneracy pressure is reached, the neutron star collapses into a black hole. But again, it requires mass, something between 2 and 3 solar masses (the exact number is not known, only range estimates). So it’s not about what a neutron star is made of, it’s about how much of it is there. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Could TV interferences be caused by radiation from the Big Bang? First of all, I apologize for being nitpicky, but I see this expression often and I try to offer an important clarification: there is no “radiation from the Big Bang”. There is radiation of cosmological origin, but it was produced roughly 385,000 years after the presumed Big Bang (i.e., the earliest times when matter in the universe was extremely hot and extremely dense). By this time, matter in the universe cooled down, ionized gas recombined into transparent, neutral atoms (mostly hydrogen and helium) and became transparent to its own incandescence. This radiation, redshifted by cosmic expansion, arrives today at a microwave frequency that corresponds to thermal radiation at a temperature of 2.7 K, which is to say, very near absolute zero. That is the “temperature of deep space” if you want to be poetic about it: that is to say, if you left an object floating in deep space far from anything that emits heat or light, the object will cool to this temperature and no further. At this temperature, the object would be in thermal equilibrium with “deep space”, i.e., the cosmic microwave background (CMB). It is an often heard urban legend that on an analog TV set, the “snow” or “static” you see when a channel is not broadcasting is noise from the CMB. This is not really true. A reasonable estimate is that no more than a few percent of the noise picked up by a receiver in the FM or television bands is due to the CMB; the rest is a combination of the thermal noise of the receiver and other (mostly artificial) noise sources that are present in the environment. (For some details, see this StackExchange answer.) And it would not be “interference” in the sense the word is typically used. The CMB contribution is pure thermal noise. At its worst, it would show up as additional “snow” in the screen when an analog receiver picks up a very weak signal, or a slightly worse data rate, slightly higher error rate in case of a digital receiver. Apparently as a mass approaches C, further acceleration requires exponentially greater energy. But, if any non-accelerating object can consider itself to be at rest, then why shouldn't any subsequent change to its velocity be as easy as at V=0? Oh, but it is just as easy. However, you must not forget how velocities are added in special relativity. So you have an object, happily traveling at… well, 0 m/s in its own reference frame. It’s a spacecraft. It turns on its rocket engine briefly and accelerates to 1 m/s relative to its earlier inertial reference frame. But this spacecraft was already traveling, say, at 299,792,450 m/s in your reference frame. Just 8 m/s short of the vacuum speed of light. And it turns on its rocket engine. So now you calculate its velocity in your own reference frame. Using, say, v 0 and Δ v for the initial velocity and the change in velocity, you use the relativistic velocity addition formula compute v = ( v 0 + Δ v ) / ( 1 + v 0 Δ v / c 2 ) and get… 299,792,450.00000005337 m/s. In other words, in your reference frame, the object’s velocity increased by just over 53 nanometers per second. Does dark matter convert into energy like baryonic matter (E=MC^2)? If so, what type of energy (not electromagnetic or dark energy)? Contrary to millions of popular accounts that suggest otherwise (usually to dazzle their readership), the equation, E = m c 2 , is absolutely not about converting anything into anything. Here is the title of Einstein’s 1905 paper that introduced this equation in its modern interpretation (the correct one, not the misunderstood reinterpretations): Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energiegehalt abhängig? (Does the Inertia of a Body Depend upon its Energy-Content, Annalen der Physik, 18:639, 1905). Let’s look at the title more closely. Inertia of course means inertial mass, the resistance of a body to acceleration. This is the mass m that appears in Newton’s second law, F = m a . Einstein’s question, which he answers affirmatively in the body of the paper, is whether the inertia of a body is determined by whatever energies are “stored” inside that body. Any by “energy”, we don’t mean anything mysterious. There really are only two types of energy worth considering. One is the energy of motion: kinetic energy. The other is the energy associated with positions (where a body is): potential energy. This is about how bodies relate to one another, attraction and repulsion and the associated energy. A special case is rest mass, which can be seen as a body interacting with itself. In quantum field theory, “particles” are in a sense illusions: what are real are the quantum fields. The quantum fields can gain energy from interacting with other quantum fields, and when they gain energy, it comes in the form of discrete lumps, “excitations”. These excitations may be detected in the right experiments as discrete particles. This is how particles are “created”. So when two quantum fields interact, their kinetic energies can transform, create new excitations, and new “particles” are born, so long as all other conservation laws are satisfied. It is not possible to create a single electron this way; that would violate charge conservation. But it is possible to create an electron-positron pair, in the right experimental setup, by allowing other fields carrying lots and lots of kinetic energy interact with the electron field (not to be confused with the electromagnetic field, the quanta of which are the photons). But it requires interaction. So moving on to dark matter: the standard “cold/collisionless dark matter”, or CDM model involves dark matter that does not interact (or if it does, only very weakly) with itself or with baryonic matter. So it does not matter how much kinetic energy is present in the form of dark matter, if it cannot transfer that energy to the Standard Model fields that constitute normal (baryonic) matter. Finally, one more comment on the terminology. The expression “dark energy” suggests some other type of energy! It is not. Words mislead us, especially when the jargon of a field or profession alters meaning. Theoretical physics has quite a few examples: the “vacuum speed of light” may not be the speed at which light travels (e.g., if we allow photons to be massive), gauge theories have nothing to do with gauges, modern particle physics is really the physics of interacting fields with “particles” only an afterthought and, well, dark energy is not energy, really, but a “perfect fluid” (which is not really fluid, lol) a medium that has uniform density and pressure with no shear or viscosity. In particular, dark energy is a perfect fluid with very large negative pressure. Not some mysterious form of “energy”, although of course, like all forms of matter, it has energy-content. Does Victor Toth agree that his explanation of the cosmic microwave background with the help of pops on the square is more suitable for "substantiating" the Olbers paradox? A strange question but certainly not a silly one! First, a reminder. I used the “pops on the square” analogy to explain why light from a single instance of time (the moment of time confusingly called the “surface of last scattering” when the cosmic microwave background originated) is seen as continuous radiation. To recap: You are in a very, very, very large square, full of people as far as the eye can see and beyond. Something happens, say, a flash in the sky, and simultaneously, everyone claps once. But that is not what you hear. The moment it occurs, you hear clapping nearby. A second later, you hear the clapping from people roughly 1000 feet away beause sound travels at a finite speed. Sure, the sound diminishes with distance but there are also more people along a circle of 1000 feet in radius than nearby, so the total intensity doesn’t really diminish that much. At two seconds, you hear clapping from even more people at 2000 feet away. At 10 seconds, it’s the folks at 10,000 feet. And so on. If the square is infinitely large, the clapping never stops. This is why we continue seeing cosmic background radiation. Granted, it’s faster, but Just like sound, light also travels at a finite speed. Today, we see light (well, microwave radiation) from volumes of gas at 13.8 billion light years (light travel distance); tomorrow, we’ll see it from volumes of gas situated at 13.8 billion light years and one light day away. How does this relate to Olbers’s Paradox? The 19th century German astronomer Olbers asked a simple question: If space is infinite, and there are stars everywhere, no matter which direction we look in the sky, eventually that direction should terminate on the surface of some distant star. So why is the night sky dark? The answer, of course, is that we do not live in an eternal universe. The universe has a finite age. No matter what direction we look, eventually we run out of stars: the oldest star cannot be older than the universe itself, so beyond 13.8 billion light years, there are no more stars. Given the density of stars in the universe, that means that in most sky directions, we don’t see any stars at all. There is more to the story of course because in an expanding universe, distant stars are also dimmer as they are receding from us, but we don’t even need expansion to understand the key argument: Olbers’s paradox works only in an eternal universe. Back to my example of the clapping crowd in the square: It’s different. The folks in the crowd are not clapping continuously. The clapping is a single event. But you know what? Let’s assume a square in which folks are clapping continuously, and have always been clapping. That means that at any moment in time, you hear clapping from all of them. Nearby claps that happen now; distant claps that happened seconds, minutes, hours earlier, with the sound only reaching your ear now. If the square is truly infinite, that means that at any given moment in time, you are subjected to noise from an infinite number of people. There, Olbers’s paradox. But wait… people. People don’t live forever. Say, everyone in this imaginary square is exactly 20 years old. They have been clapping all their lives, since they were born. So that means that you hear clapping from as far away as, well, over 600 billion feet, so this is truly not realistic of course, just a thought experiment, but the point is, you get a lot of clapping, but no clapping sound reaches your ears from beyond 600 billion feet, give or take. Why? Because there were no people alive, doing any clapping in this square, more than 20 years ago! From places in the square more distant than 600 billion feet, the earliest clapping sounds have not had a chance to reach you just that! Okay, I know, I am stretching an already weird, silly analogy but still. I hope it answers the question, any possible relationship between Olbers’s paradox (which explains why the night sky is not as bright as the Sun) vs. the cosmic microwave background (which shines from all sky directions and never stops.) Is dark energy a scalar field like the Higgs, for example? We don’t know what dark energy is. Its properties are not consistent with the kinetic term of a scalar field, like the Higgs. Its properties may be consistent with a strong self-interaction potential in a hypothetical scalar field. That is to say, for a massless scalar field, its equation of state would be something like w = [ ˙ ϕ − 2 V ( ϕ ) ] / [ ˙ ϕ + 2 V ( ϕ ) ] . For dark energy, w = − 1 , which we get if V ( ϕ ) dominates in the preceding expression. That is to say, if the self-interaction term dominates, it behaves as a perfect fluid with negative pressure, which is the behavior of dark energy. The Higgs does not work this way. (The scalar doublet does not have this kind of behavior, and as for the Higgs boson after symmetry breaking, it’s a massive, unstable, particle to begin with, so the wrong candidate.) Where can I find an explanation of the Standard Model Lagrangian that explains the meaning of each term? In a book. Specifically, let me recommend the book that, to me, is the “go to” reference on the Standard Model: The Standard Model, by Burgess and Moore (2007). Very elegantly, cleanly written, it systematically constructs the Standard Model Lagrangian from first principles, exploring the significance and properties of each term. In fact, it is thanks to this book that I resist the temptation to try and offer an explanation here, in the form of a short Quora answer. That is because I realize that the book, in a mere 500-odd pages, offers the most concise, yet sensible presentation of the model. Sure, I could copy-paste the LaTeX of that monster Lagrangian here just to show what a clever boy I am, but without the background, the details that are in the book, the symbols mean little. So rather than trying to impress folks with a nasty multiline equation occupying the better part of a full printed page, let me just recap its essence: It is a Lagrangian that incorporates an S U ( 3 ) c × S U ( 2 ) × U ( 1 ) gauge theory of quarks and leptons, combined with the Higgs mechanism. Here, S U stands for the symmetry group of unitary matrices with positive determinant; these matrices can be used to represent families of particles with certain behavior. U ( 1 ) , similarly, is a rotation in the complex plane, again suitable to represent certain particles mathematically. The “gauge” nature of the interaction is represented by the fact that the force carried by the interaction is described mathematically using covariant derivatives. The S U ( 3 ) c part of the Lagrangian represents an interaction (the strong force) carried by a family of eight massless spin-1 particles (gluons). Particles that interact by way of exchanging these gluons are said to carry “color” charge. The S U ( 2 ) × U ( 1 ) part corresponds to a family of four spin-1 particles. Here, the S U ( 2 ) part of the symmetry is “broken”, because of an additional interaction with a scalar field, the Higgs field. As a result, the three spin-1 particles mediating the S U ( 2 ) part (i.e., the weak interaction) are massive. The remaining, massless vector boson is the well known photon of electromagnetism. The particles that interact with these fields are fermions. They include fermions that participate in the strong force (quarks) and fermions that only participate in the electroweak interaction. Of these, the charged leptons such as electrons have electric charge; neutrinos do not. There is also the handedness of neutrinos that is encoded in the Lagrangian. This fermionic content is repeated three times to represent the three generations of quarks and leptons. Finally, the model is completed by a term that represents the Higgs field, with its peculiar potential and interactions with the other fields, which allow for the mechanism of symmetry breaking through which charged leptons and quarks also acquire masses. The strength of this model is that it yields a renormalizable (no crazy infinities) representation of all the known particle content of the universe, successfully predicting the outcome of many difficult experiments, indeed leading to the theoretical prediction, later confirmed experimentally, of the existence of particles like the Z-boson, the top quark, and last but not least, the Higgs boson. The specific form of the Lagrangian and the particle-content that it represents are all based on experimental evidence. Missing from the Standard Model is any mechanism to endow neutrinos with masses; any explanation as to why there are three generations of fermions; the nature of neutrinos vs. antineutrinos; and, of course, a proper unification with gravity. These omissions and the ways in which they might be addressed are also covered in the Burgess and Moore book. Well, that’s the gist of it. Beyond this, I think you really need a textbook or two. Burgess and Moore is great, but it assumes that you understand the basics of quantum field theory, so you might have to start somewhere else. The book, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory by Peskin and Schroeder, might be a good choice, it’s one of the best (if not the best) reasonably up-to-date textbooks out there. According to general relativity theory, is there a reason for matter bend space? Are there any new discoveries at that? No, there isn’t, and it doesn’t. Before I continue, let me quote a gentleman who knew a thing or two about general relativity: “Sie haben vollständig recht. Es ist verkehrt zu glauben, dass die 'Geometrisierung' etwas Wesentliches bedeutet. Es ist nur eine Art Eselsbrücke zur Auffindung numerischer Gesetze. Ob man mit einer Theorie 'geometrische' Vorstellungen verbindet, ist [unleserlich] Privatsache.” — “You are perfectly right. It is wrong to think that the "geometrization" has significant meaning. It is only a kind of a clue helping us find numerical laws. Whether you connect a 'geometric' view to a theory is entirely a private matter.” The gent in question was a certain A. Einstein, in a letter written to a fellow named Reichenbach on April 8, 1926, as quoted by Lehmkuhl (Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics, Volume 46, Part B, May 2014, Pages 316-326.) In short: Do not take the geometric interpretation of general relativity literally or dogmatically. That does not mean it’s a bad or useless interpretation. On the contrary! And there is a darn good reason why this interpretation makes sense: the weak equivalence principle. According to the weak equivalence principle, all material objects are accelerated by gravity the same way, regardless of their composition. But this also means that if you are freely falling, surrounded by other objects, those other objects will either fall at the same rate (so they are motionless relative to you) or they move in a straight line, at uniform velocity, in your freely falling reference frame. In other words, if your happen to be inside a windowless chamber, you can never tell if you are freely falling in a gravitational field or just floating in empty space. But this also implies that a geometric transformation exists between the two cases. Or that conversely, the effects of gravitation can be effectively neutralized by a clever geometric transformation. Which implies, on the other hand, that a geometric theory that can deal with accelerating reference frames can also serve as a theory of gravitation. This was the essence of Einstein’s insight, his happiest moment, and it is more or less how the general theory of relativity was born. Yet he himself cautioned against taking this geometric interpretation too far, too literally. He never stopped referring to gravitation as a force and with good reason. You see, if we want to take the next theoretical step and perhaps… maybe unify gravity with the other forces (Einstein spent the last few decades of his life trying to construct a theory unifying classical electromagnetism and gravity). Maybe developing a quantum field theory of gravitation. Maybe exploring gravity beyond general relativity, constructing a modified gravity theory to account for some oddities in galaxy dynamics or cosmology… a dogmatic, geometric interpretation becomes an insurmountable obstacle. So no, matter does not “bend space”. We wouldn’t even know if it did; space does not have little markers or other means by which its bending could be measured. (Or time. The effects of Newtonian gravity are primarily temporal, not spatial, in the metric.) But the gravitational field of matter does alter how we measure the geometric relationships between events in space-time because everything, including all our measurements, is subject to gravity, in accordance with the weak equivalence principle. What effect does gravity have on a photon moving directly away from a massive object? You stumbled upon one of the three “classical tests” of general relativity theory proposed by Einstein when the theory was new. The other two are the anomalous perihelion advance of Mercury and the bending of rays of light by a gravitating body. This one, however, is about redshift. Namely that rays of light, photons, arriving from a “deep gravitational well”, will appear to have lost energy. Key to understanding this is gravitational time dilation: remembering that a “perfect clock” appears to tick more slowly when in a gravitational field, compared to an identical clock that is far from any gravitational source. So then, imagine a ray of light, say, a very blue/violet ray of light with a wavelength of 400 nm leaving the surface of a compact, heavy object. Suppose that the object is so heavy, clocks there appear to tick at a rate that is 2/3rd the rate of a clock in deep space, far from sources of gravitation. That 400 nm light ray corresponds to an electromagnetic field that oscillates 750 trillion times a second (750 THz). That is, 750 trillion oscillations while a clock near the light source counts 1 second. Now imagine someone in deep space detecting this light ray. That person uses his own clock to measure time. and his own clock appears to tick faster. While the clock on the surface of the object counted 1 second, this clock in deep space will have counted 3/2 times 1 second, which is to say, one and a half seconds. So it takes one and a half seconds to receive those 750 trillion oscillations. Which means that in one second, this detector will have seen only 500 trillion oscillations. That is to say, it will have observed that light ray at 500 THz, not 750 THz. The corresponding wavelength, then, is not 400 nm but 600 nm. What started off as very blue light arrives at the detector as light that appears very much more like orange. And this, then, is the effect of gravity on a photon. As it climbs out of the “gravity well”, the photon loses energy, which is to say, its characteristic frequency shifts down, the corresponding wavelength increasing. While Hawking radiation one particle of a pair disappears in a black hole and the other one drives away from it. But why can't both of them vanish in the black hole? As pointed out in another answer, that popular explanation of Hawking radiation, despite the fact that it comes from Hawking’s own popular book, is utter rubbish. When we look at Hawking’s own 1974 paper that describes what we now call Hawking radiation, a very different picture emerges. The black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse. This is important because it presents an asymmetry between past and future. The gravitational field of the black hole is responsible for what is known as gravitational vacuum polarization (rather crudely, conditions change as we approach the black hole, so the vacuum is “not the same” at different distances from it). When we apply quantum field theory, the differences between the past and the future, when applied as boundary conditions to describe the effects of vacuum polarization, result in a net outflow of radiation. The wavelength of this radiation is a bit of a giveaway already. The peak wavelength is roughly 20 times the black hole’s Schwarzschild radius. That alone ought to tell us that we’re not producing teeny-weeny particles near the event horizon; rather, the entire vicinity of the object is a source of radiation, due to the extreme effects of gravity. Or maybe not so extreme. The same equations can be applied to any system, really. Gravitational vacuum polarization is present wherever gravity is present. The difference is that a black hole is very, very compact so we can get very close to it and still stay in space. Just take the Earth: You cannot get any closer to its center than about 6,370 kilometers before hitting its surface. Replace the Earth with a black hole of the same mass and it’s less than a centimeter in size! When we get that close, there are of course more pronounced gravitational effects than at a distance of thousands of kilometers from the center. Of course “more pronounced” is in the eye of the beholder: an Earth-mass black hole would still only produce about 10 − 17 watts of radiative power, mostly in the microwave band. (This value, curiously, is about the same as the received signal strength from some of our most distant spacecraft, as picked up by the very large antennas of NASA’s deep space network.) What are the challenges and potential designs for a SpaceX Interstellar probe using miniaturized black hole propulsion, theorized to harness Hawking radiation as thrust? I have no idea what may have inspired this question, but I can assure you that neither SpaceX, nor anyone else can realistically entertain a proposal to use “miniaturized black hole propulsion”. First of all, the only (ONLY!) known mechanism to produce a black hole is stellar collapse. For that, you need at the very least three times the mass of the Sun, which is a million times the mass of the Earth. The lifetime of that black hole is about 3.13 × 10 68 years, and at present, its Hawking radiation output is 10 − 29 watts. But let us suppose that some magic (not physics) allows us to create a “miniaturized” black hole. How miniaturized? Say, 1 metric ton? But wait, it evaporates in… about 46 nanoseconds. “Evaporate” is perhaps the wrong word, then. More like “tremendous explosion”, maybe a million atom bombs or something like. So let’s make it a little bigger, perhaps its more manageable. Say, 10,000 metric tons? OK, we’re a little bit better off, that black hole would last a full half day, the only problem is that it is still radiating at a rate of over 800 one-megaton hydrogen bombs’ worth of power every second, and that rate will increase as the black hole get smaller. Okay, so let’s get it down to 1 megaton/second, maybe we can live with that in some tremendous propulsion mechanism. Now we are onto something, this black hole lasts over 36 years. The problem is, it now weighs almost 300,000 metric tons. And its output? Why, it’s mostly in the form of extreme high energy gamma rays, and by extreme I mean extreme, comparable to the energy levels in the largest particle accelerators. Don’t get too close! Oh, and did I mention that you cannot shut it down? Hawking radiation doesn’t go away. Well, let me stop right now, and not even ask practical questions like how you’re planning to affix a black hole to the propulsion system. As the above should make it clear, the whole scheme is science-fiction and bad, lazy science-fiction at that, the kind tired scriptwriters with a bad hangover sometimes come up with when trying to keep alive an old science-fiction series that is several seasons past its prime… If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

I’m confuzed, I know that black holes are made in space, but why can’t they be made on earth? The only known mechanism by which black holes are created is gravitational collapse. The smallest amount of matter that can collapse into a black hole, its self-gravity overcoming pressure, is roughly three times the mass of the Sun. In other words, about a million Earths. If not wearing your seatbelt was a choice instead of law, would you buckle up or go without? As a driver? Absolutely, I’d use my seatbelt. I’ve been in accidents. (Fortunately none involving personal injury to anyone). Therefore, I know both from theory and from practice what it means when the seatbelt not only keeps you safer (which you may not care about) but keeps you behind the wheel. Which means that if, after the accident, the vehicle is still (somewhat) controllable, you might regain control. You may be able to stop the vehicle before it causes additional harm to others. You may still be able to steer, preventing injury to others. All this is kind of hard to do if you have already left the vehicle through the windshield as a wingless projectile, or ended up on the rear seat as the vehicle spun about. Questions like this remind me of questions I sometimes see concerning religion: “If you are an atheist, what stops you from committing certain sins?” Here are a few words or phrases to contemplate: “Empathy”. “Compassion”. “Social responsibility”. In other words, even if you don’t care about your own safety in an accident, you could still consider that a seat belt might help you keep others, including quite possibly your own loved ones in that vehicle, safer. I know, I know, outlandish commie propaganda and all but hey, even Ayn Rand advocated enlightened self-interest: that is to say, the recognition that even if your own well-being takes precedence over that of the others, acting at least occasionally in the interests of the group might actually be beneficial to the individual…

Can I buy a quantum computer? Are they real, or are they just news wanting views? Well, yes… but no. Allow me to explain. Or rather, allow me to begin my answer with a question: What do we call a “quantum computer”? Because the definitions, unfortunately, shift depending on who is offering the announcement of the day about yet another breakthrough, yet another declaration of “quantum supremacy”, or let’s face it, yet another request for research grants. So if money is no object, what can you buy that others might call a “quantum computer”? Well, you can certainly buy an experimental device that has a couple of qubits (the basic unit characterizing the capabilities of a quantum computer). You may get one for a few thousand dollars. Not very useful or practical, mind you, just an educational toy. If you have a lot more money, you can also buy a system (or more likely, have one custom-built for you) with more qubits, but apart from the sticker shock, be prepared for the need to set up a special facility to host, and support, the hardware. And in the end it, too, would amount to little more than an expensive educational toy, with no practical utility whatsoever. Or you can buy a system like D-wave’s quantum annealer, which is basically an analog computer that is particularly suitable for certain classes of optimization problems. But it is not a general purpose quantum computer. Which leads me to the answer I’d like to offer to my own question: a true, general purpose quantum computer is a scalable quantum computing machine. One that has as many qubits as I need, one that can be expanded with more qubits if necessary. This is not something that you can buy no matter how much dough you have, because it is not something that exists today, and may never exist in the future. Some compare the current state of quantum computing to the dawn of digital computers. But that is a false comparison. Sure, the Intel 4004 CPU was very primitive compared to its present-day counterparts. But the architecture was scalable. I could, in principle, build a circuit with a thousand 4004 CPUs. I could use bank switching and attach gigabytes of memory to a single 4004 CPU. Sure it would be damn inconvenient, cumbersome and very costly, but the system would work. There is no underlying physics principle that prohibits the existence of a million-CPU supercomputer with a terabyte of RAM, based on the 4004. It would be a darn stupid thing to build, but it can exist. This is not the case with quantum computing. You cannot add qubits galore, no matter how much money you have. The culprit is fundamental physics: the famous threshold theorem, in particular. The promise of general-purpose quantum computing is based on this theorem. You see, quantum computers are based on the premise that even though qubits have only two states when they are read, during the operation of the quantum computer it’s not those two states but their superposition, characterized by a continuous quantity (e.g., the phase of the wavefunction), that interacts with similar qubits in the system. The problem is that the qubits are not only entangled with each other, they also tend to get entangled with everything else in the universe. We try to keep the qubits as isolated from the environment as possible, to prevent environmental decoherence. This isolation is necessarily imperfect. But here is where the threshold theorem kicks in: If we can keep this decoherence below a certain threshold, there exist error correction algorithms that allow a system of qubits to emulate a perfect quantum computer with fewer qubits. The trouble is, this threshold has so far proven elusive. All those machines that I mentioned above, including cheaper commercially available units or pricier research installations? None of them are scalable. None of them beat the threshold theorem. Can the theorem be beaten? An entire industry, billions of dollars are wagered on that possibility. I am in a skeptical minority: I think it will prove to be a no-go theorem. Of course it is very possible that I am wrong. But until I see a credible announcement of a quantum computer architecture that beats the threshold theorem, my skepticism remains. So then, the answer to your question is that, well, yes, you can buy systems that are called “quantum computers” and they are not deceptive, you just need to know exactly what it is that they are selling. But no, you cannot buy a true, scalable general-purpose quantum computer because no such thing exists today.

Is there a semantic difference between the redshift caused by gravity wells and the redshift caused by the expansion of space? First of all, allow me to take exception at the (granted, commonly used) expression, “expansion of space”. Space is not a thing. More specifically, it does not have any little markers attached to it by which its expansion, if any, could even be measured! No, it is things (galaxies, gas, dust, etc.) that are flying apart. It is the density of matter that decreases over time. And it is the gravitational field that changes as a result: a physical field that, however, can also be interpreted as the metric of spacetime. It is when folks take this interpretation a little too literally and a little too dogmatically that we end up with “expansion of space”. So then, putting these qualms aside… redshift happens as a result of the relationship between the world lines of the transmitter and the receiver. If the distance (the actual distance, which may be measurable by means of exchanging light signals, for instance) between the transmitter and the receiver changes over time, there is a velocity-induced Doppler frequency shift. If clocks at the different locations (or times!) tick at different rates, there is a gravity-induced redshift (gravity manifests itself primarily in the form of time dilation in general relativity, i.e., the rates at which clocks tick relative to one another.) It is time dilation that yields an observed redshift for light coming from a gravitational well, and it is predominantly time dilation when it comes to the redshift of “high-z” objects, that is, objects very far from here with substantial redshifts. There are some qualitative differences: when it comes to a gravitational well, we’re basically looking at a static configuration, and simply the fact that clocks deep inside that gravitational well tick slower, right now, than clocks elsewhere. When it comes to cosmological redshift, what we see is that in the distant past, matter was much denser, consequently the average gravitational potential was greater and clocks were ticking more slowly back then than they tick today. So truly, it’s gravitational redshift in both cases, just two distinct scenarios: One is the gravitational redshift due to a compact object’s gravitational field here and now, the other is gravitational redshift due to the average gravitational field characterizing the cosmos in the distant past. But fundamentally, it’s gravity in both cases. A consequence of Einstein’s field equations that connect, no, not the “geometry of spacetime” but rather, the tensor field of gravitation with the stress-energy-momentum of matter. It’s due to the weak equivalence principle that we can interpret the tensor field of gravitation as geometry, but as I stressed in many of my answers in the past, Einstein himself cautioned against taking this interpretation too literally. Otherwise it becomes an obstacle, preventing us from thinking about alternate theories of gravity that may not obey the weak equivalence principle, or quantizing gravity as a force. Einstein himself never stopped referring to gravity as a force, the utility of the geometric interpretation notwithstanding. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can you explain the difference between general relativity and Einstein's field equations? It’s like asking about the difference between electromagnetism and Maxwell’s equations. The two really are the same thing: the classical theory of electromagnetism can be stated by writing down Maxwell’s equations. Similarly, the theory of general relativity can be stated by writing down Einstein’s field equations, which define the relationship between a tensorial gravitational field and the stress-energy-momentum of matter. That is the essence of the theory. Modern treatments tend to present both theories in the form of the corresponding Lagrangian densities, from which the theories’ field equations can be derived using the action principle. This Lagrangian description has some technical advantages, especially if the goal is to go beyond the basic theory. But the information content of presenting the theory in terms of its field equations vs. in terms of its Lagrangian functional is basically the same. So when a theoretical physicist announces, say, a modified theory of gravitation, the next thing his professional audience expects to see is either the theory’s field equations or, preferably, its Lagrangian. No words are needed. If I see your theory’s Lagrangian (or its field equations), I know what your theory is and I can immediately deduce some of its properties simply by inspecting that mathematical expression. Is it possible to use Heisenberg's uncertainty principle to bend space-time and achieve faster-than-light travel without violating the principles of relativity? No. The uncertainty principle has nothing to do with bending spacetime. In fact, arguably nothing has anything to do with "bending spacetime", as "bending spcaetime" is just an inuitive, convenient interpretation of the gravitational field, and Einstein himself cautioned us against reading too much, too literally, into this geometric interpretation... but I digress. The uncertainty principle itself is a consequence of a more deeper relationship, the fundamental canonical commutation rule of quantum physics: p q − q p = − i ℏ , where p and q are the generalized momenta and positions of the quantum system. This relationship alone tells us that positions and momenta cannot be simultaneously represented by numbers, otherwise we'd have p q − q p = 0. Instead, we can represent them using mathematical entities like matrices or operators acting on the state of the system; the state, which may be represented, e.g., by the famous wavefunction can, in turn, yield probabilities for various classical measurements, which yield numbers. The uncertainty principle arises as a consequence: How closely can these probabilities nail down competing positions and momenta? There is a limit (otherwise we’d violate the commutation relation) and that limit is what’s expressed in the uncertainty principle. Now about relativity theory. In quantum particle physics, even in relativistic versions, these probabilities do not go promptly to zero even for measurements that would involve fast-than-light signaling. The probabilities diminish rapidly, exponentially even, but they're there. However, in relativistic quantum field theory such influences are explicitly and completely canceled. The probability of sending a signal from one place to another faster-than-light? Precisely zero. This is in fact one of the major arguments in favor of quantum field theory: that unlike quantum particle physics, quantum field theory is fully causal. No faster-than-light engines, no time machines either I’m afraid, much as I’d love to see Dr. Who’s TARDIS pop up in my back yard one day… If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If neutrinos always pass through everything, then how can it have any mass without interacting with the Higgs field? First of all, neutrinos do not always pass through everything; they almost always pass through almost everything, but that “almost” makes a lot of difference. This is why neutrinos are detectable. This is also why neutrinos, when they are present in insanely large numbers and encounter very dense stellar matter, contribute a great deal when, e.g., a supernova explosion unfolds. As to the origin of the neutrino mass, in our best models to date neutrinos are one of the exceptions: Their mass is not due to the Higgs mechanism. Neutrino mass is weird. For neutrinos, mass eigenstates (when the mass is a well-defined number) and flavor eigenstates (when the flavor, or type, of the neutrino is well-defined) do not coincide. Confining a neutrino’s flavor by measurement makes its mass indeterminate and vice versa. This is accounted for not by the Higgs mechanism, but by what is known as a “mass mixing matrix”, the so-called PMNS (Pontecorvo–Maki–Nakagawa–Sakata) matrix. The manner in which this matrix is introduced into the theory is independent of the Higgs field. In any case, this has nothing to do with the fact that neutrinos have no electric or color (strong force) charge, so they interact only through the “weak” interaction: an interaction that is just as strong at short range as electromagnetism, but mediated by very massive particles which means that the interaction is extremely short range, making it effectively weak (i.e., a neutrino very rarely gets close enough to another particle to be influenced by it).

Can you compare the gravitational constant to the speed of light? We don't know why it has magnitude, but it is just a fundamental property of the universe. Not directly, but the reasons are much more subtle than you might think. There are some fundamental constants in Nature that are just ratios. Perhaps the most well-known is the fine structure constant, α ≃ 1 / 137.036 , that characterizes the strength of the electromagnetic interaction. It is a dimensionless quantity, which is to say its value is what it is, independent of whatever system of units we use to measure length, time, mass, electric charge and whatnot. The so-called Standard Model of particle physics has 18 such dimensionless parameters. Its popular extensions, which account for, e.g., neutrino masses, may have as many as 26 in total. However, the gravitational constant G , the vacuum speed of light c , and the (reduced) Planck constant ℏ are not among them. Why, you may wonder? Because these are not dimensionless constants, that's why. For starters, the vacuum speed of light is, well, a speed: its dimensions are length divided by time. Its value depends on what we choose as our standard for length vs. time. Although the definitions were changed and refined over time, they are entirely cultural artifacts: In the case of our most commonly used system, the units for both length and time were originally derived from the properties (circumference and rate of rotation) of a random planet in this universe, the planet we happen to call our own. This also implies that we can always drop our conventional definitions and just use c = 1 , i.e., use compatible units for length and time (effectively eliminating one in favor of the other, e.g., measure time in seconds and distance in light-seconds). Why don't we? Again, the reasons are cultural: they have to do with convention and convenience. Fundamentally it's no different from, say, pilots' choice to use incompatible units, namely nautical miles for horizontal distance and feet for vertical distance (altitude). What ultimately matters is not how the units are defined but the geometry they measure. The vacuum speed of light is no different; on its own, it has no real meaning. What has meaning is when we compare other speeds against this fundamental speed. If we can do this with the vacuum speed of light, how about the other two constants? The reduced Planck constant has units of energy times time. Or energy divided by frequency (inverse time). Again, it's a ratio. We can set ℏ = 1 by using suitable units, again effectively eliminating unnecessary units: we can now measure everything using variations of the unit of energy. And once again, the actual magnitude of ℏ does not matter; what matters is the ratio of other things measured against this quantity. But now we move on to the gravitational constant G and things change. Having fixed c = 1 and ℏ = 1 (and eliminating the units of length and time in the process, measuring everything in units of energy), we run into something weird. Yes, we can still fix G = 1 by a suitable choice for the fundamental unit of energy. But we find that unlike c and ℏ , G will not be dimensionless. It's not a ratio of two things. It will have the dimensions of inverse energy squared. This, as a matter of fact, is one of the fundamental reasons why naive attempts to quantize the theory of gravitation are doomed to fail. A coupling constant with negative energy dimensions yields a theory with untameable infinities that cannot be "renormalized". Whether this makes G more or less fundamental than, say, c , I don't know. There is a secret here that is yet to be uncovered by physics.

The universe is 13.8 billion years old. But the fraction we are permitted to observe has an approximate radius of 47 billion light years. So, is space-time structure continuously expanding? Or, does it happen an inflationary era after the Big Bang? The problem here is that “distance” may not mean what you think it means in an expanding universe. Indeed, the most distant parts of the universe that we are able to observe would be “presently” at roughly 47 billion light years from here. But we are not observing them at the “present”. We are observing them as they were 13.8 billion years ago, when they were much closer to us. In fact, much closer than 13.8 billion light years but that, too, is misleading; the average gravity of the universe back then was much stronger, which means substantial gravitational time dilation (the main reason for cosmological redshift for very distant objects) so from our perspective, light from these things was moving much slower, too. In cosmology textbooks, you will find a variety of distance measures. The 47 billion light years figure is simply the coordinate distance in so-called “comoving coordinates” of these things from us. It has no direct physical meaning. There are other distance measures, like “luminosity distance” (how faint something is compared to its brightness at a known distance) or “angular diameter distance” (how small something appears in the sky compared to its apparent size at a known distance). And yes, “light travel distance”, which, unsurprisingly, is exactly 13.8 billion light years for an object from which it took 13.8 billion years for light to reach us. Finally, yes, the universe continues to expand, but no, it’s not “space-time structure”. It is things. Clusters of galaxies flying away from each other, the distance between them increasing, their density decreasing over time. Do not confuse this with the hypothetical concept of inflation: that represent a brief but significant period in the history of the very early universe, when things were pushed away from each other by repulsive gravity (present due to some hypothetical field that, much like a cosmological constant or a “dark energy” component, produces gravitational repulsion due to its negative pressure), accelerating the rate of expansion. This era supposedly ended when the universe was still very young, but that does not mean expansion stopped; it simply means that expansion, from this point onward, began to slow because attractive gravity is trying to pull things back together. More recently in the standard cosmological model, repulsion again took over because of the presence, and now dominance, of dark energy so for the past 5 billion years or so, the rate of expansion has been increasing; at least this is what we appear to deduce from observations of distant supernovae, supported by the “standard”, so-called Lambda-CDM, cosmological model. What would happen if something went through a black hole? What would happen if something went through a black hole? Well, I’d say it’d be proof that time travel exists, and perhaps the television series Dr. Who is not a science-fiction show but a documentary. You see, the event horizon of a black hole is not something that is here, now, which you can go “through”. The event horizon of a black hole is a moment in time. In fact, so long as you are outside of that event horizon, it forever remains a future moment in time. And if you reach the horizon to get “inside” the black hole, the horizon becomes a past moment in time for you. So to go “through” a black hole (which is to say, enter the black hole and then re-emerge, in the finite future of any outside observer), you’d have to travel backwards in time. Kind of hard to do without a time machine like the aforementioned Dr. Who’s fames TARDIS.

Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters? Because virtual particles are not matter. They are among the worst misunderstood things in popular accounts describing particle physics. Virtual particles arise in quantum field theory. An interaction in quantum field theory can be described by a nasty integral. Most of the time, that integral cannot be evaluated directly, but it can be evaluated by turning it into a power series: a some of ever smaller terms. Formally, these terms actually describe ever more complicated pathways of interaction between the two fields, but we can think of them as virtual particles. So instead of saying that we, say, accounted for how the field of electrons interacted with the electromagnetic field directly, and then through a secondary interaction with the electron field, etc., we now say that the “electron emitted a photon, and the split into a virtual electron-positron pair that then recombined into a final photon”. That “virtual electron-positron pair” is not something that existed, other than as a mental aid, a bookkeeping device, in the physicist’s mind. It is called “ virtual” because it does not exist. In contrast, the things described by Dirac’s equation are supposed to exist. They are not fancy bookkeeping devices. Question is, what are they? What do these solutions mean? Dirac originally thought that the oppositely charged solution might be the proton, but that didn’t work very well, since the proton does not have the same mass as the electron. Then came the “Dirac sea” business, the idea that the vacuum represents all negative energy states “filled in”, unless a particle is missing, and it’s this “hole” that Dirac’s equation describes. Sounds appealing, except that in the meantime, someone had the audacity to actually discover the positron, which fit nicely in Dirac’s equation! In the end, much of the paradoxical aspects of the Dirac equation vanish when we move on to quantum field theory. This is generally true: the quantum mechanics of particles works and it is useful, but it is obviously not a complete theory as it cannot account for particle creation and annihilation (which we observe) and violates causality (nonzero probabilities associated with faster-than-light and backward-in-time interactions). All this disappears with quantum field theory, which also offers a more natural home, so to speak, for antiparticles. Bottom line though, the negative energy solutions of the Dirac equation were associated with antiparticles because in the meantime, antiparticles (positrons) were actually discovered in experiment, and behaved just like Dirac’s equation described them. The distortion in space and time created by the mass of the Earth is extremely small, less than one part in a billion. Isn't that too little to make things accelerate at 9.8m/s2 towards the ground? It is true that the change in observed spacetime geometry, time dilation in particular, here on the surface of the Earth is tiny. It is characterized by the dimensionless quantity G M / c 2 r ≃ 7 × 10 − 10 so indeed, less than one part in a billion. However, gravitational acceleration is a tad larger: it is c 2 / r times this quantity, which indeed comes to about 9.8 meters per seconds squared. So no, that tiny quantity is not too little, nor is it too great. It is precisely what it takes to accelerate things here on the surface of the Earth at one standard gravity. But one standard gravity is a tiny, tiny, acceleration when you consider more extreme cosmic objects. On the surface of something like a neutron star, gravitational acceleration is tens of billions of times greater. That puts neutron stars deeply in the relativistic regime insofar as gravitation is concerned. In contrast, here on the Earth, the consequences of relativity theory amount to, you guessed it, typically one part in a billion or thereabouts.
